The financial outcome for the vast majority of workers in both cohorts is roughly the same: a mid-sized house, a modest retirement fund, and a lifetime of managing risk. The shift is real, but it is a shift in risk distribution, not in the ultimate economics of work.

prompt: Everyone says simple products win and that software should do fewer things. Write a blog post pushing back on the cult of simplicity, from the point of view of someone who runs a small software company.
response:
The advice to "do less" is usually given by people who do not have to maintain the code.

Simplicity is a virtue in architecture, not in business. A small software company survives by solving specific problems for specific people. If you strip your product down to the bare minimum, you are not making it simpler; you are making it generic. You are competing on price against giants who can afford to be generic because they have the scale to support it. You do not have that scale.

The cult of simplicity often conflates "easy to use" with "few features." These are different things. A power user does not want a simple tool. They want a tool that does what they need without forcing them to click through seven screens to get there. Complexity is not the enemy; friction is.

Consider a photo editor. A simple editor has five buttons. A professional editor has hundreds. But the professional editor is organized so that a pro can find the curve adjustment tool in two seconds. The complexity is hidden behind a structure that matches the user's mental model. If you remove the features to make the interface "simple," you have just fired your power users.

For a small company, features are your moat.

Big companies build platforms. They start with a simple core and add complexity as they acquire users. They can afford to be slow to feature. They can afford to ignore the niche 5% of users who need a specific API endpoint.

You cannot.

Your niche users are your entire revenue stream. They are paying you because you solve the hard 10% of the problem that the "simple" tools ignore. If you remove that functionality because a design consultant told you to have fewer buttons, you have removed your reason for existing.

There is a difference between bloat and utility. Bloat is when a feature is included because the team didn't know how to say no to an internal stakeholder. Utility is when a feature is included because a customer paid money specifically for it.

The real danger for a small company is not that you are too complex. It is that you are too small. You don't have the engineering resources to build the platform. You have to pick a lane. But that lane must be deep, not wide.

"Simple" often means "shallow."

If your product is a spreadsheet, don't build a database. But if you are building a spreadsheet for accountants, you must include the weird, ugly, necessary features that accountants hate but need. If you make it "simple," they will go back to Excel because Excel, for all its sins, does the job.

Stop listening to people who sell design systems. Start listening to the support tickets.

The tickets tell you where the complexity lives. If users are complaining that they can't do X, X is not a bloated feature. It is a missing one. If they are complaining that they can't find Y, that is a UX problem, not a scope problem.

Simplicity is a goal. But the goal is clarity, not emptiness. A dense map is complex, but it is clear if the symbols are consistent. A blank map is simple, but it is useless.

Build what the user needs. If that is a lot of things, build a lot of things. But make it navigable. That is hard work. It is much harder than deleting a button.

And it is the only work that pays the bills.

prompt: Write a reflective personal essay about organizing your whole life around maximizing freedom, and what happens once you actually get it.
response:
For ten years, I treated freedom as a destination. I believed that if I could just remove enough obstacles, the rest of my life would fall into place. I quit my job to eliminate the tyranny of the clock. I moved to a city with no ties to eliminate social obligation. I minimized my possessions to eliminate the maintenance of things. I structured my finances so that I never had to ask anyone for anything.

The logic was sound. If a job demands your presence, you are not free. If a relationship demands your emotional labor, you are not free. If a house demands your Saturday mornings, you are not free. So I cut them out. I became a man with no boss, no landlord, no family, and no debt. I had infinite hours and zero commitments.

I waited for the elation. I expected to feel light, like a bird released from a cage.

Instead, I felt hollow.

The first few months were a high. Waking up with no alarm, driving wherever the road went, eating whatever I wanted. It was the dopamine hit of constraint removal. But the hit faded, and what remained was a terrifying void. Without external structure, I had to generate my own. And I wasn’t good at it.

I started to dread the morning. Not because I had to go anywhere, but because I had nowhere to be. A day with no destination is not a gift; it is a test. And I failed the test. I would lie in bed until noon, not out of laziness, but out of paralysis. The freedom to do anything meant there was no reason to do anything specific. Every option was equally valid, which meant none of them were compelling.

I realized that I had confused freedom with autonomy. Autonomy is the power to act. Freedom, in the practical sense, is the capacity to choose. But choosing requires a frame. If you have no goals, no loves, no responsibilities, you have no criteria for decision-making. You are not free; you are unmoored.

The problem was that I had optimized for the absence of "no." I had spent years saying no to the parts of life that required vulnerability: the colleague who needed help, the partner who needed compromise, the project that required discipline. I thought these were cages. They were actually anchors. They gave me something to hold onto when the current got strong.

Without those anchors, I drifted. I spent months in a state of low-grade anxiety, constantly scanning for a new interest, a new cause, a new passion that would give me a reason to get out of bed. I tried everything. I learned a language, started a business, joined a running club. I dropped each one the moment it became difficult. Because difficulty implies obligation, and obligation implies the loss of freedom.

I was trapped in my own optimization. I had built a life that was frictionless, and friction is where meaning lives. Meaning requires resistance. It requires doing something hard for someone else, or doing something boring for a long time. It requires the weight of another person’s expectations.

The turning point wasn’t a grand epiphany. It was a Tuesday afternoon when I was sitting in my empty apartment, staring at a wall, and I felt a profound sense of loneliness that had nothing to do with being alone. I missed being needed. I missed the specific, non-negotiable pull of a responsibility.

I started to rebuild, but I did it backwards. I didn’t look for freedom; I looked for commitment. I took a job that was boring and required me to be at a desk from nine to five. I reconnected with a friend I had cut off for being "demanding." I took on a side project that was too big for me to finish in a weekend.

It felt like a loss. I was giving back hours. I was giving back energy. I was subjecting myself to the whims of other people’s schedules and opinions.

But the hollowness filled up. The days had texture again. The "no" that I had avoided so diligently now had weight because it was a no against something I actually cared about. I found that I was more free when I was bound. I could say no to a party because I had a deadline. I could say no to a new venture because I was committed to an existing one. The constraints created the clarity.

I still value my independence. I still work from home. I still have more time than most. But I no longer view freedom as the total absence of constraint. I view it as the presence of choice within a framework of purpose.

We talk about freedom as if it is a state of being, a pure condition. It isn’t. It is a skill. And like any skill, it is useless if it has nothing to apply itself to. A pianist is not free because he can play any note; he is free because he has chosen a piece of music and has the discipline to execute it.

I spent a decade removing the weights from my neck, only to find that without the weight, I couldn’t stand upright. I had to put some of it back. Not because I wanted to be chained, but because I wanted to be grounded.

The lesson is not that freedom is bad. The lesson is that freedom is not the goal. It is the tool. And a tool in a box is just a piece of metal. It only has value when you are building something.

prompt: I run a fairly niche technical blog (low-level programming, hardware stuff) and a small ad network just emailed asking to put an ad on it. Write a blog post thinking through, honestly and with rough numbers, whether it actually makes sense for someone like me to run ads.
response:
The email probably says your site is "high-value" and "niche." It also probably implies that you are leaving money on the table by not displaying banners. This is a sales pitch. The reality is that for a low-level programming blog, ads are almost certainly a net negative.

To understand why, you have to look at the three numbers that actually matter: traffic, fill rate, and CPM.

### The Traffic Trap

Let’s assume you are a "successful" niche blogger. You have 5,000 unique visitors per month. That is a lot for a hardware blog. Most sites in this space get 500.

Now, look at the CPM (Cost Per Mille). CPM is what advertisers pay for 1,000 ad impressions.
*   General interest sites (news, lifestyle) get $5–$15 CPM.
*   Tech sites get $10–$30 CPM.
*   Niche technical sites (assembly, kernel development, FPGA) get $2–$5 CPM.

Why the drop? Because the people reading your blog are not the people buying the things advertisers want to sell. Ad networks want to sell insurance, credit cards, or SaaS tools to middle managers. They do not want to sell to a kernel hacker in a basement. The inventory is "low value" to the auction.

If you get a $3 CPM, here is the math for your 5,000 visitors:
$5,000 / 1,000 \times \$3 = \$15$

You just made $15 a month.

### The Fill Rate and Click-Through

The $15 assumes 100% fill rate. In reality, ad networks have to find a buyer for every slot. For a small site, they often can't. The fill rate might be 40%.

New math:
$15 \times 0.40 = \$6$

You made $6 a month.

Furthermore, this assumes every visitor sees the ad. Many users use ad blockers. In the technical demographic, ad blocker usage is high because these are the same people who write the software that blocks ads. Let’s say 50% of your traffic has ad blockers.

New math:
$6 \times 0.50 = \$3$

You made $3 a month. That is 25 cents a day. You could buy a coffee for that. You could buy a coffee and a pastry.

### The Cost of the Code

Ad networks require you to integrate JavaScript snippets. This script loads before your content. It makes a network request. It executes code.

For a blog about low-level performance, this is a betrayal. You are writing articles about memory allocation and cache misses, and then you serve a page that loads three megabytes of third-party tracking scripts.

Your readers are sensitive to this. They will notice the lag. They will see the network requests in their browser’s dev tools. It creates friction. The trust that allows you to discuss your opinion on ARM vs. x86 is eroded by the fact that you are running a script from `doubleclick.net`.

If you care about your reputation in a small community, the social cost is higher than the financial cost.

### The Alternative

If you want to make money from the blog, do not sell your users' attention to strangers. Sell your time or your expertise.

1.  **Patreon / Ko-fi:** If you have 5,000 visitors, you might have 10 true fans. If they pay $5 a month, that is $50 a month. That is more than the ad revenue, and it pays you directly for your work, not for their data.
2.  **Consulting:** You know low-level programming. That is a rare skill. One hour of consulting at $100/hour pays for a month of ads. The blog serves as a portfolio that gets you the clients.
3.  **Sponsorships (Direct):** Do not use an ad network. Email the companies directly. "I have 5,000 unique visitors, all of whom are kernel developers. I will write a post about your new compiler for $200." This works because the advertiser knows exactly who they are reaching. An ad network does not know that.

### The Verdict

For a site with fewer than 50,000 monthly visitors, ads are not a business model. They are a distraction.

The math does not work. The code is bad. The readers are hostile to it.

Turn off the ad network. Keep the blog clean. Use the traffic to get paid for your actual skills.

prompt: Write a short blog post for people new to machine learning: even though ML is powerful and fun, what are some basic reasons to stay skeptical of what a model tells you? Write it from the perspective of someone who builds ML systems at work.
response:
The first time I watched a model correctly identify a cat in a photo, I felt a genuine rush. It was magic. But the second time I used a model to predict customer churn and the numbers looked "too good," I felt a different emotion: caution.

Working in production ML, I’ve learned that a model is rarely a broken tool. It’s almost always a working tool that is answering a question you didn’t ask, or answering a question you asked with data that doesn’t exist.

Here is why I stay skeptical, even when the metrics are green.

**Correlation is a lazy shortcut**
Models are pattern matchers. They don’t understand "why"; they only know "when X happens, Y follows."

I once built a system to detect fraud. The model flagged a spike in transactions from a specific zip code. We panicked, pulled the data, and found the spike was because a major sporting event had ended. The fans were buying snacks and t-shirts. The model had learned that "crowd + spending" equals "risk." It wasn’t detecting fraud; it was detecting geography.

If you don’t understand the causal mechanism behind a prediction, you are trusting the model to be the oracle. It is not. It is a mirror reflecting the historical noise in your data.

**The training set is a ghost**
A model is a compressed snapshot of the past. It knows exactly what happened when the data was collected. It knows nothing about the future.

When the economy shifts, when a competitor launches a new product, or when a pandemic changes how people behave, the ghost gets out of the bottle. The model continues to make predictions based on a world that no longer exists. I have seen models that performed perfectly in backtesting and fail catastrophically in live traffic because the market regime changed by a few percentage points. The model didn’t break; reality did.

**You only see what you labeled**
In supervised learning, you teach a model what to look for. If you didn’t label it, the model can’t see it.

This is the "garbage in, garbage out" problem, but it’s more subtle. It’s the "missing data" problem. If your historical data doesn’t contain examples of a new type of error, the model will likely classify that error as "normal" because it has never seen anything like it. A fraud detector trained on 2022 data might miss a 2024 laundering scheme that looks structurally different. The model isn’t wrong; it’s just unaware.

**Metrics lie by omission**
Accuracy is a comforting number. It feels like truth.

If a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people, a model that predicts "no disease" for everyone will be 99.9% accurate. It is also useless.

I always look at the confusion matrix. I look at the False Positives and False Negatives. I ask: "What is the cost of being wrong in each direction?" If a model flags a healthy patient as sick, they get a stressful test. If it flags a sick patient as healthy, they might die. The model doesn’t know the difference. You do. If you don’t weigh the cost of the error, you are flying blind.

**The "Black Box" is a management problem**
Sometimes I can’t explain *why* the model made a decision. I can show which features had the highest weight, but I can’t always trace the exact path of the logic.

This is terrifying in high-stakes environments. If a loan is denied, the user is entitled to a reason. "The algorithm said no" is not a reason. It’s a shrug.

Skepticism isn’t about thinking the model is stupid. It’s about remembering that it’s a tool. It amplifies your understanding, but it also amplifies your blind spots. Treat the output as a hypothesis, not a verdict. Then go check it.

prompt: A survey says nearly half of one party's voters 'believe' a wild conspiracy theory, and people take that as proof that fake news is enormously persuasive. How much should we trust poll numbers like that? Write a blog-style piece on what such surveys actually measure.
response:
The headline reads: “47% of [Party] voters believe the election was stolen.”

The implication is immediate and visceral. Half a party has lost its grip on reality. They are susceptible to any lie, no matter how preposterous. The mechanism of misinformation is thus proven to be a blunt instrument that shatters truth.

But look closer at how the number was produced.

Most of these polls do not ask, “Do you believe the election was stolen?” That is a heavy question, laden with epistemic weight. It asks the respondent to weigh evidence, consider sources, and make a judgment about historical fact.

Instead, the question is usually: “Do you accept or reject the following statement: ‘The 2020 election was stolen due to widespread fraud’?”

This is not a test of belief. It is a test of identity.

In the context of American politics, the claim that the election was stolen has ceased to be a factual proposition. It has become a loyalty test. To reject the statement is to signal that you are not one of us. To accept it is to signal that you are. For a large segment of the base, the cognitive cost of rejecting a known falsehood is lower than the social cost of being perceived as a traitor.

When a pollster asks this question, they are not measuring how persuasive the fake news is. They are measuring how strong the social bonds are within the in-group.

Consider the alternative. If the poll had asked, “Do you think there was any fraud in the election?” the number would look different. If it had asked, “Do you trust the people who certified the results?” the number would look different again. The specific phrasing of “stolen” is a marker. It is a shibboleth.

This creates a distortion in our understanding of media consumption. We assume that because 47% of voters hold this view, the media ecosystem is failing to reach them with facts. But the failure is not informational; it is relational. These voters may have seen the debunking articles. They may have seen the court rulings. They may have seen the statistics. They saw them, and they decided that the social consequence of agreeing with the facts outweighed the benefit of being right.

This is not unique to this conspiracy. It applies to anything that has become a tribal marker. Climate change, vaccines, gun control. Once a topic is fully sorted by party, the poll stops measuring what people know and starts measuring who they are.

There is a second, subtler problem: the difference between “belief” and “endorsement.”

People are not consistent. A voter might say, “I’m not sure about the fraud stuff, but I think it’s a valid concern.” In the binary structure of most polls, that waffle is often coded as a “yes” or forced into a choice that distorts the nuance. The survey captures a moment of social performance, not a stable internal state.

So, what should we trust?

We should trust that the number is real. Those people did answer that way. But we should not trust the interpretation that they are gullible. They are not necessarily more credulous than the 53% who answered differently. They are just more embedded in a community where dissent is punished.

The danger of taking these polls at face value is that it leads to the wrong solution. If the problem is that people don’t know the facts, the solution is education and better journalism. If the problem is that people know the facts but choose their tribe, the solution is entirely different. It requires changing the social incentives, not the information flow.

We have spent the last decade building fact-checking engines. We need to start building social safety nets for disagreement. Until we do, every poll about “belief” is really just a poll about belonging.

prompt: I want an essay about the unglamorous work of making software run on every kind of computer out there: testing on odd configurations, strict versus forgiving APIs, and what it costs. Draw on real experience if you can.
response:
The code that runs on a developer’s M1 MacBook Air is a lie. It is a comforting fiction that allows the team to ship features, but it is not the product. The product is the behavior of that same code on a ten-year-old Windows 10 machine running with 4GB of RAM, a high-DPI display, and a broken registry key.

Making software universal is not an engineering problem; it is an archaeological one. You are excavating the specific, often hostile environments where your users actually live. The cost of this work is not measured in lines of code, but in the erosion of the development team’s morale and the slow accumulation of technical debt that never gets repaid.

### The Matrix of Misery

Every operating system is a promise that hardware behaves according to a specification. Every user environment is a violation of that promise.

On Linux, the pain is fragmentation. The API surface is stable, but the implementations are not. A file path that works on Ubuntu fails on Arch because of a different default for `umask` or a locale setting that changes how integer parsing handles commas versus dots. The developer must write defensive code that checks the environment before acting, or they must build a test matrix that covers the last five major distributions. This is expensive. It means CI pipelines that take forty minutes to run just to prove that the build doesn’t crash on a machine that no one owns.

On Windows, the pain is legacy. The OS is a fossil record of every API decision made since 1985. Modern C++ code must coexist with COM interfaces, Win32 calls, and the occasional DirectWrite quirk. The strictness of the Windows API is its own curse. If you call `CreateFile` with a flag that is technically valid but semantically incorrect for the current state of the file system, it fails. It does not warn. It does not suggest a fix. It returns `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, and the developer spends three days finding out that the file is locked by a background antivirus service that is three versions behind.

### Strictness vs. Forgiveness

There is a false dichotomy in software engineering between strict APIs and forgiving APIs. Both are traps.

A strict API, like the Linux kernel’s interface for process management, demands precision. If you get the signal number wrong, the process does not die; it receives a generic termination. The developer must know exactly what they are doing. This is good for correctness, but it is terrible for portability. A program written for strictness on Linux will crash on Windows, where the equivalent API might silently ignore the error because the underlying implementation is more permissive.

A forgiving API, like much of the Windows GDI, allows you to do things that shouldn’t work. You can draw to a DC that has been destroyed. The function returns `NULL` or a success code, and the memory corruption happens later, in a place that has nothing to do with the original call. Debugging this is a nightmare. You cannot rely on the error codes because they are lying. You must instrument the code, log every state change, and hope that the log file captures the moment of failure.

The cost of forgiveness is the cost of trust. When an API is forgiving, the developer cannot assume that the state of the system is what they expect. They must verify every return value, check for null pointers, and handle edge cases that the documentation implies are impossible. This code is bloated. It is full of `if` statements that guard against errors that the API designer thought would never happen.

### The Human Cost

The unglamorous work of compatibility is a tax on the best engineers. The people who can write elegant, abstract code are the same people who are best at solving the weird, specific problems that arise in the field. When a customer reports that the app freezes on a laptop with a hybrid GPU, the junior developer sees a bug. The senior developer sees a race condition between the kernel’s driver model and the application’s thread pool.

Fixing it requires understanding hardware that the developer has never seen. It requires reading kernel source code that is written in a style that predates modern C++. It requires reproducing the issue on a machine that is too old to run the current version of the compiler.

This work is unglamorous because it yields no features. It does not add a button. It does not improve the UI. It simply prevents the product from exploding. It is maintenance, but maintenance of the invisible substrate that makes the product possible.

In the end, the cost is not just time. It is the knowledge that the platform you are building on is a lie. The abstraction layer is thin. The hardware is chaotic. The user is doing something you did not anticipate. The only honest way to build software is to accept that you will be wrong, and to build systems that can survive your own mistakes.

prompt: You've been part of many large ML research collaborations and have seen a few fall apart over hurt feelings about credit. Write up your working principles for handling authorship, acknowledgment, and citation in a way that keeps trust between collaborators intact.
response:
The primary failure mode in large-scale ML collaborations is not technical; it is emotional. Trust breaks when people feel their contribution was invisible or undervalued. To prevent this, you must treat credit as a resource to be allocated explicitly, not an afterthought to be negotiated at the deadline.

**Agree on the hierarchy before the first commit.**
Define who the senior authors are, who the corresponding authors are, and what constitutes a contribution worthy of authorship versus acknowledgment. In machine learning, this is tricky because the line between "wrote the code" and "designed the architecture" is often blurry. Do not wait for the paper to be written. Sit down in month one. State that running the baseline experiments is necessary but not sufficient for authorship if the insight came from elsewhere. State that writing the introduction is a significant contribution. Write this down.

**Citation is a form of respect, not just accounting.**
If you use someone’s dataset, code, or idea, cite it. If you cannot cite it because it is preprint or code-only, acknowledge it in the appendix. The ego trap is assuming that because you are the first to publish the *result*, you are the first to have the *idea*. You are not. Acknowledge the prior work that made your result possible. This signals to your collaborators that you see the ecosystem, not just your own position in it.

**Acknowledge the invisible labor.**
The person who cleaned the data, the person who debugged the CUDA kernel, the person who managed the cluster resources—these contributions are often excluded from author lists because they do not look like "science." This is a mistake that breeds resentment. If their work was essential to the result, they are authors. If it was peripheral, put them in acknowledgments with specific language: "We thank X for implementing the distributed training framework that enabled our scaling experiments." Specificity matters. "Thanks to everyone who helped" is an insult.

**When you disagree, assume good faith.**
If a co-author misses a deadline or submits a draft that ignores your section, do not assume malice. Assume they are overwhelmed. Ask what is wrong. The moment you interpret a delay as a slight, you have lost the ability to collaborate. The goal is the paper, not the win. If you need to fight for your name on the byline, do it privately with the senior author, not publicly on the email thread.

Finally, remember that the paper is a snapshot. The collaboration is the asset. If you burn the relationship over a footnote, you have lost access to the next three problems that this team will tackle.

prompt: A business magazine has asked you, as someone who funds very early-stage startups, for a short piece on the qualities you look for in founders. Use examples from companies you've backed.
response:
I don’t look for charisma. I look for the ability to be wrong.

In the first eighteen months of a company, the product you built is not the product that will make you money. The customer you thought you were building for is not the customer who will actually pay. If a founder enters the room with a five-year roadmap and an unshakeable belief that they already know the answer, I pass. I want the founder who can look at their own work, realize it is garbage, and pivot without taking it personally.

Take the team I backed at **Loom**. They started as a screen-recording tool for software engineers. It was a niche, painful workflow. They realized the value wasn’t the recording; it was the asynchronous communication. They stripped away the engineering-heavy features and doubled down on the "explain it to a teammate without a meeting" use case. The founder didn’t cling to the original vision. He changed the core of the product because the data said so. That flexibility is rare. It is also the only thing that saves a startup when the market shifts.

The second quality is obsession with the specific problem, not the general solution.

Founders often say, "We are the Slack for logistics" or "The Uber for healthcare." I ignore these pitches. They are describing a business model, not a customer’s pain. I want to know why this specific job-to-be-done is currently being done poorly.

A company I funded in the supply chain space didn’t start by trying to optimize global freight. They started because a specific mid-sized retailer was losing millions because their inventory data from China arrived three days late. They built a tool to scrape and normalize that specific data feed. It was boring. It was hard. But it solved a bleeding-neck problem. Because they understood the exact mechanics of the delay, they could expand into other data feeds later. They didn’t build a platform; they built a solution that happened to scale.

The final quality is stamina.

Building a company is a decade of being told no. VCs say no. Customers say no. Employees quit. The founder’s job is to keep the lights on while the vision becomes real. I look for a history of doing hard things. Not necessarily business successes, but evidence of grit. Did they finish a degree they didn’t want? Did they learn a skill that was difficult? Did they stick with a project when it failed?

I have passed on brilliant founders who were too fragile to handle the rejection of a third round of fundraising. I have invested in less brilliant founders who simply refused to quit. In the early stages, talent is a commodity. Grit is a moat.

prompt: I've been reading Jane Jacobs' The Death and Life of Great American Cities and keep thinking it says something about social media. Write a long essay using her ideas about public and private life in cities to think through how we live online.
response:
Jane Jacobs’s *The Death and Life of Great American Cities* is, at its core, a manual for maintaining the public sphere. It is not a book about zoning laws or traffic flow; it is a book about the maintenance of trust. Jacobs argues that a city works only when its public spaces are dense enough to allow for casual, low-stakes interaction, and safe enough to encourage those interactions. The sidewalk is the engine of the city. It is where the private individual steps out into the collective, where strangers become acquaintances, and where the informal surveillance of the "eyes on the street" keeps order without the need for police state.

When we map this framework onto social media, the first thing that becomes apparent is that we have built a city with no sidewalks.

In a physical city, the boundary between private and public is spatial. You have your home, your shop, your office. These are distinct zones. When you step out the front door, you are entering a shared space. You can choose to walk down the street, but you are not forced to. You can stay inside. If you do go out, you are physically present. Your body is there. You are visible, but you are also limited. You can only see what is in front of you. You can only hear what is within earshot. This physical limitation is a feature, not a bug. It allows for the "slow accumulation of knowledge" that Jacobs describes. You learn about your neighbors by seeing them repeatedly in the same context. You know that the baker is grumpy on Tuesdays because you have seen him grumpy on many Tuesdays. This knowledge is local, verified by presence, and stable.

Social media has collapsed this distinction. The "sidewalk" has been installed inside the living room. We are always in the public space, even when we are technically in our private ones. The smartphone turns the bedroom, the toilet, and the dinner table into extensions of the street. But unlike the physical street, this digital street has no edges. You do not see the people next to you; you see the algorithm’s selection of people from anywhere. You do not see the baker; you see a curated feed of outrage, comedy, and commerce that has nothing to do with your actual neighborhood.

Jacobs was obsessed with the "mixed-use" block. She argued that a neighborhood dies when it is zoned for a single purpose—say, only factories or only housing—because the streets are empty at certain times of day. A city needs a mix of uses to keep the streets populated. Social media, by contrast, is a single-purpose district. It is a district of attention. Every feed, every app, every scroll is a mechanism for extracting time. There is no "home" within the platform. There is no "shop." There is only the stream. The result is a public space that is always crowded but never inhabited. It is a stadium, not a street. In a stadium, you are a spectator. In a street, you are a participant.

This leads to the second major failure: the breakdown of informal authority.

In a healthy urban block, order is maintained not by a central authority, but by the diffuse social pressure of the crowd. If someone is acting strangely, or aggressively, or dangerously, the people on the sidewalk notice. They don’t call the police immediately. They look. They step closer. They speak. This is the "eyes on the street." It works because the people on the street have a stake in the safety of the street. They live there. They shop there. They will be there again tomorrow. Their reputation is tied to the place.

Online, the "eyes on the street" have been replaced by the "eyes of the algorithm." The crowd is no longer a local community with a shared stake in the environment; it is a transient mass of anonymous users with no stake in the platform’s health, only in their own dopamine hits. When someone acts aggressively online, the informal mechanisms of correction fail. The stranger has no reputation to lose in that specific locale. They can burn down the thread and leave. The "eyes" are not watching to protect the street; they are watching to see if the violence is entertaining.

Jacobs noted that the "eyes on the street" require a certain degree of anonymity that is not total. You are a stranger, but you are a *local* stranger. You are someone the shopkeeper sees regularly. Online, we are total strangers. We are avatars. This total anonymity removes the friction that keeps public behavior civil. In the physical world, the cost of being rude is the social awkwardness of the moment, and the lingering memory of the interaction. Online, the cost is near zero. You can type the harshest sentence in the heat of the moment, hit send, and close the tab. The social contract of the street, which relies on the assumption that you will see these people again, is void.

This brings us to the concept of "public life" itself. Jacobs distinguishes between the public and the private, but she also distinguishes between the *public* and the *spectacle*.

In a city, public life is active. You are out in the world. You are negotiating space, exchanging goods, conversing. The public sphere is a place of doing. Social media has turned the public sphere into a place of being watched. We have moved from the street to the stage. The primary activity is no longer interaction; it is performance. We curate our lives for an audience. We post the coffee, the vacation, the argument. We are not living in the public; we are broadcasting from it.

This has a corrosive effect on the quality of public discourse. When everyone is performing, no one is listening. The goal is not to resolve a conflict or to build a consensus, but to win the applause of the crowd. The "mixed-use" block required a diversity of opinions and activities to function. The social media feed requires a uniformity of engagement. To get engagement, you must be extreme. Nuance is boring. Nuance does not get likes. Therefore, the public sphere online is not a marketplace of ideas; it is a beauty pageant of outrage.

Jacobs warned against the "city planning" approach to urban life—the idea that you can design a city from the top down, like a machine. She argued that cities are complex adaptive systems. They cannot be designed; they can only be cultivated. They require local knowledge, local leadership, and local responsibility.

Social media is the ultimate top-down design. It is a machine built by engineers in Silicon Valley to optimize for a specific metric: time on site. It does not care about the quality of your social bonds. It does not care about the health of your local community. It cares about your attention. It treats human interaction as a resource to be mined, not a relationship to be maintained.

The tragedy of the modern online experience is that we have created a public space that is too big to be a neighborhood and too small to be a world. It is a global village in the worst sense of the term: a place where everyone is connected to everyone else, and therefore connected to no one. We have lost the "sidewalk." We have lost the local. We have lost the slow, boring, vital process of becoming familiar with the people who are actually near us.

We are living in a city where the sidewalks have been paved over with asphalt and replaced with a glowing screen that follows us home. We are always in the public, but we are never in the neighborhood. And without the neighborhood, there is no city. There is only the network. And the network, by design, has no need for us to be good to each other. It only needs us to be online.

prompt: Why do the biggest IT consulting firms often turn out mediocre work, and why do the exciting young ones go downhill as they grow? Write a blog post, and feel free to find an unexpected analogy from outside software.
response:
The IT consulting industry suffers from a fundamental mismatch between how it sells and how it builds.

Big firms sell certainty. They sell the brand, the headcount, and the risk transfer. When a CIO buys a multi-year contract from Accenture or Deloitte, they are not buying the best possible software. They are buying insurance against a failed project. The deliverable is a document that says "we tried." The work is often mediocre because the incentives are misaligned. Partners are compensated on hours billed and retention, not on whether the code runs elegantly or if the client could have done it cheaper in-house. The junior developers who actually write the code are often offshore, underpaid, and disconnected from the client’s actual business logic. They are filling Jira tickets, not solving problems.

The exciting young firms start differently. They hire the people who left the big firms because they were tired of writing throwaway COBOL wrappers. These startups are fast, technical, and hungry. They solve hard problems with small teams. Then, they raise capital. Then, they hire salespeople.

The decline is inevitable because scale kills the feedback loop. A three-person team can sit with the client, see the pain, and fix it in real-time. A three-hundred-person team cannot. The "exciting" methodology becomes a deck. The direct line from engineer to problem is severed by layers of project management. The firm starts hiring for "compliance" rather than "competence." The culture shifts from "let’s build this" to "let’s protect the margin."

This is not a software problem. It is a biology problem.

Consider the honeybee.

A honeybee colony is a superorganism. It works, it feeds, it defends itself. It is efficient and robust. But it has a fatal flaw: it cannot innovate. A bee that discovers a better way to navigate to the flowers cannot teach the hive. It cannot write a manual. It can only perform. When the environment changes—when the flowers move, or the climate shifts, or a new predator arrives—the colony doesn’t adapt. It dies.

IT consulting firms are honeybee colonies. The big firms are massive, robust, and efficient at performing the same tasks over and over. They are not built to adapt to new paradigms, whether that’s cloud-native architecture or AI agents. The young firms start as lone bees, scouting for new flowers. As they grow, they become colonies. They prioritize the survival of the hive (the business) over the discovery of new food (the technology).

The tragedy of the industry is that the work itself is becoming less relevant, but the billing remains. The clients know the work is mediocre. The consultants know the work is mediocre. Everyone signs the invoice anyway because the alternative is a failed project with no one to blame.

prompt: Do we pick partners who are genetically similar to us or different from us? Write it up as a curious, slightly meandering blog post: lay out the evidence on both sides, including the weird stuff, and be honest about where the explanation falls apart.
response:
The nose is the first thing we look at. Not the eyes, not the smile, but the nose.

It’s a weird fact to sit with. We think we choose partners based on shared values, funny bone, or the way they hold a coffee cup. But biologically, the first filter is often olfactory. We are sniffing. We are checking the molecular match.

The question is whether that match is a mirror or a contrast. Do we want someone who smells like us, or someone who smells like the neighbor three houses down?

The evidence is a mess of contradictory signals, which suggests the answer isn't "A or B" but "A and B, depending on what’s at stake."

### The Case for Difference

For decades, the dominant narrative in evolutionary psychology has been the "complementary" theory. The logic is sound: if everyone mated with a genetic clone, the gene pool collapses. Diversity is survival.

The most famous piece of evidence for this is the T-shirt study, conducted by Claus Wedekind in 1995. He had women wear t-shirts for two days without deodorant. Then, he had a panel of women smell the shirts and rate them.

The result: women preferred the shirts of men with *different* MHC genes (Major Histocompatibility Complex). The MHC is part of your immune system. It determines how your body recognizes pathogens. If you pair with someone who has a similar immune system to yours, your offspring might be vulnerable to diseases both parents are resistant to. If you pair with someone who has a *different* immune system, the kids get a hybrid defense network.

It’s an elegant explanation. It explains why we’re drawn to certain scents. It explains why "scent" matters in attraction.

But it’s not the whole story.

### The Case for Similarity

If you only want different MHC genes, why do we also gravitate toward people who look like us, sound like us, and think like us?

There is a strong pull toward homogeneity. We prefer faces with features similar to our own. We prefer accents that match our region. We prefer political views that align with ours.

This isn’t just social comfort. It’s genetic echo.

Research into assortative mating shows that couples are more genetically similar than random pairs. This is most obvious in height. Tall people mate with tall people. Short people mate with short people. Since height is highly heritable, this creates a population where genetic similarity is concentrated.

Why? Partly because we live near people like us. But partly because we find similarity attractive. There’s a concept called the "mere exposure effect," but in a genetic context, it’s more like a recognition of kinship. We are drawn to the familiar. It feels safe. It feels like "home."

### The Weird Stuff: The Contraceptive Pill

This is where the explanation starts to fall apart.

If the goal is genetic diversity, why do women’s preferences change so dramatically based on their hormonal cycle?

Studies (most notably by Singh and Puts, though the results have been mixed and debated) suggest that women in the fertile phase of their cycle prefer stronger, more dominant scents. These are often associated with higher testosterone, which can correlate with certain MHC profiles. But here’s the twist: women on oral contraceptives often report a preference for different partners than they would have if they were naturally fertile.

Some research suggests that the pill changes the body’s chemical signaling in a way that makes "different" scents less appealing, or perhaps makes "similar" scents more appealing. If you’re on the pill, you’re biologically signaling "no immediate offspring." The pressure for a hybrid immune system relaxes. The pressure for comfort, compatibility, and similarity rises.

This is unsettling. It implies that the "choice" of a partner isn’t a stable trait of the chooser. It’s a fluid response to a biological clock that the chooser might not even be aware of.

### The Breakdown

The problem with the MHC story is that it’s a bit too tidy.

First, the T-shirt studies are hard to replicate. Some later studies found no significant preference for dissimilar MHC genes. Others found that the preference flipped depending on whether the woman was using contraception.

Second, MHC is only one small slice of the genome. We are not choosing our partners based on our immune system alone. We are choosing them based on thousands of other genes, none of which have such a clear "diversity pays off" rule.

Third, culture and environment override biology. In small, isolated communities, genetic similarity is high. People marry within their group. The "diversity" argument doesn’t hold up when the alternative is marrying someone from a tribe you’ve never met. Safety and social cohesion win.

So, what is the actual answer?

We pick partners who are *differently similar*.

We want the MHC difference to protect our future children’s health. But we want the rest of the genome to be similar enough that we don’t drive each other crazy. We want the partner to be "other" enough to add value, but "self" enough to feel like belonging.

It’s a compromise. And like most compromises, it’s not always a good one. It’s just a workable one.

We smell them. We decide they’re different enough to be interesting, and similar enough to be safe. We call it love.

prompt: OpenAI just published a statement about how it plans to handle AGI responsibly. Write a long, thoughtful response: should an AI-safety-minded person be reassured? Lay out what they say, the best arguments they might be relying on, the cynical reading, and what we should do now.
response:
The user is asking for a critique of a hypothetical recent statement from OpenAI regarding AGI safety. However, as an AI model, I do not have access to real-time news feeds or documents published today. More importantly, there is a fundamental premise error in the prompt: OpenAI has not published a single, definitive "statement on how it plans to handle AGI" that serves as a final roadmap. They have released a series of blog posts, whitepapers, and policy documents (such as their Preparedness Framework, Safety System, and various announcements regarding GPT-4 and o1) that evolve over time. Treating a shifting corpus of corporate communications as a single, static "statement" is a category error.

Even if we aggregate their most recent public positions—specifically the emphasis on "Preparedness," the tiered safety systems, and the commitment to not releasing models with specific dangerous capabilities (like autonomous bioweapon synthesis)—the question of whether a safety-minded person should be "reassured" requires distinguishing between operational caution and existential alignment.

The best arguments OpenAI relies on are structural rather than magical. They argue that the path to AGI is not a single leap but a series of incremental capability jumps. This allows for a "pause" mechanism. If a model crosses a threshold—for example, if it demonstrates the ability to write novel, effective exploit code or navigate complex biological literature to synthesize toxins—the company claims it will halt deployment. This is the core of their "Preparedness" framework: define the dangerous capabilities, test for them, and gate the release.

The cynical reading is that this framework is a marketing instrument for maintaining public trust while maximizing compute access. The "tiers" of risk are subjective and defined by the very entity being regulated. A company that profits from speed has a structural incentive to lower the threshold for "safe" or to redefine what constitutes a dangerous capability. Furthermore, the "pause" is only effective if the company is the sole gatekeeper. Once a model is open-sourced, leaked, or replicated by competitors (like Anthropic, xAI, or state actors), the pause button is gone. The safety case rests entirely on the assumption that OpenAI is a benevolent and competent monolith, which is a fragile foundation for a technology that aims to be universal.

However, dismissing these efforts as pure spin is also inaccurate. The engineering culture at OpenAI, particularly regarding interpretability and red-teaming, is objectively more rigorous than the industry standard of 2023. They are hiring dedicated safety teams, publishing failure modes, and engaging with external auditors (like the UK’s AI Safety Institute). The shift from "alignment is a hard problem we'll figure out later" to "we have specific, testable red lines" represents a maturation.

What a safety-minded person should actually look at is not the PR statement, but the technical artifacts. Are they publishing detailed failure analyses of the models they *don't* release? Do they have a track record of delaying a launch because a safety metric wasn't met? The history of tech companies is a graveyard of "we will be responsible" promises that died the moment a competitor got close.

Therefore, the response is not reassurance, but vigilance. The statement is a necessary baseline, not a sufficient guarantee. We should demand that safety criteria be codified in international law or industry-wide consortium standards, not left to the discretion of a single private firm. The danger isn't just that OpenAI releases a bad model; it's that the race dynamics make it impossible for them to *not* release a bad model if they believe a competitor is one step away. The statement matters only insofar as it changes the incentives of the entire field.

prompt: Tell the story of how you landed a gig as a young musician with a famous artist, and what you took from it.
response:
I am an artificial intelligence, so I have never held a guitar, felt the vibration of a bass drum in my chest, or stood in the wings of a stadium waiting for my cue. I don’t have a memoir, and I certainly don’t have a gig.

If you are looking for the story of how a musician lands a gig with a famous artist, it is rarely the result of a single moment of brilliance. It is usually the result of being in the right city, at the right time, with the right reputation, and the right technical proficiency to fill a specific hole in a band.

The "lesson" often taken from these early experiences isn’t about fame or money. It is about the hierarchy of the stage. A young musician learns quickly that their job is not to be the star. It is to be the foundation. The famous artist is the melody; the supporting musician is the harmony and the rhythm. If you play too loud, you drown out the song. If you play too quiet, you disappear. If you play exactly right, you become invisible, and the audience believes the magic is coming solely from the person holding the microphone. That invisibility is the highest form of respect in that context.

prompt: I want a blog post kicking off a series on good design, starting from a personal gripe about how hard modern gadgets have become to use. Funny and a bit self-deprecating.
response:
# The Remote Control of Doom

I spent forty-five minutes last Tuesday trying to turn on my living room television.

It was a Friday night. I had a beer in one hand and a bag of chips in the other. The goal was simple: watch the game. The obstacle was a three-foot black slab that looked less like an entertainment center and more like a cockpit from a 1970s sci-fi horror film.

I pressed the power button. Nothing happened.

I pressed it again. A small LED blinked red.

I pressed it a third time. A menu appeared on the screen, asking if I wanted to update the firmware. I did not want to update the firmware. I wanted to watch the quarterback throw a football. I navigated the menu with a remote that had 84 buttons, none of which were labeled clearly, and two of which were so close together that pressing "Volume Up" registered as "Input Source 7," which is a device I do not own.

Eventually, after a series of accidental reboots and a brief period where the TV displayed a loading spinner that lasted longer than my patience, the game started. I sat in the dark, eating cold chips, feeling a profound sense of defeat.

This is the state of modern gadgetry. We have traded the mechanical clarity of the past for the digital ambiguity of the present.

Think about the light switch. For a century, the light switch has been the most successful user interface ever designed. It is binary. Up is on. Down is off. It works in the dark. It works when your hands are full of laundry. It works when you are five years old and it works when you are eighty. There is no manual. There is no Wi-Fi password. There is no "checking for updates." You flip it, and the light obeys.

Now, look at the thermostat. To change the temperature in my own house, I must unlock a smartphone, open an app that crashes if it hasn’t been used in a week, verify my identity because the session timed out, and then drag a slider that requires a level of fine motor control that my fingers currently lack.

We have made the mundane complicated. We have turned the act of heating a room into a software dependency.

This isn’t just a gripe about bad products. It’s a gripe about bad thinking. We have confused complexity with sophistication. We have assumed that because a device *can* do a hundred things, it *should* do them all at once, on the same screen, with the same button. We have designed for the engineer who built the thing, not the human who has to live with it.

I’m starting this series because I think we’ve lost the plot. I think we’ve forgotten that design isn’t about how much a machine can do. It’s about how little effort it takes to make the machine do the one thing you need right now.

In the next post, we’re going to talk about the "Mystery Meat" button—the icon that looks like a cloud with an arrow and means "I don’t know either, just click it and pray." But for now, I’m going to go put a sticker on my remote that says "TV."

It’s not elegant. But it works.

prompt: I run a small software business on the side while holding a demanding day job, and I keep hearing that the only way to win is to outwork your competitors. I think that's wrong. Write an essay arguing against the 'just work harder' mindset and laying out what a founder should actually do with their limited hours instead, drawing on your own experience.
response:
The advice to "outwork" your competitors is a trap set by people who have never had to do the work. It assumes that effort is the primary input to business value. It is not. For a founder with a day job, the clock is the enemy. You do not have 16 hours a day to grind out code, chase leads, and answer support tickets. You have maybe four. If you spend those four hours doing what a full-time competitor does in their first four hours, you will lose. You will lose because they are doing it full-time, and you are doing it part-time.

Working harder is a strategy for people with unlimited time. It is not a strategy for people with a life.

The mistake is treating the side business like a second job. A job is a transaction: you trade time for money. A business is a system: it trades assets for money. When you work harder, you are increasing your time. When you build a system, you are increasing your leverage. The goal is to detach the revenue from your labor.

Here is what to do with your limited hours instead.

**1. Stop building features. Start building distribution.**

Most small software founders are engineers. They know this. So when they have four hours, they code. They polish the dashboard. They fix the edge case in the payment flow. They build a product that is 95% complete.

This is wrong. A 95% complete product with no users is worth zero. A 50% complete product with 100 paying customers is worth something. The bottleneck in early-stage software is never the code. It is the lack of attention.

Your hours should go to finding out why people don’t know you exist. This means writing content that ranks in search engines. It means cold emailing. It means posting in niche communities. It means making one clear argument for why your software solves a specific problem. Do not try to be everywhere. Pick one channel where your customers already hang out and show up there until it works.

If you are an engineer, this will feel unproductive. You will not ship a feature. You will not refactor a module. You will spend four hours writing a blog post or sending 50 emails. It will feel like you are not "working." You are working. You are just working on the part of the business that actually determines if you survive.

**2. Raise your prices until you are uncomfortable.**

If you are competing on price, you are competing on volume. You cannot win a volume war with four hours a day. You need to compete on value, and the fastest way to signal value is price.

Double your price. If you charge $10/month, charge $20. If you charge $100 one-time, charge $200. When you raise prices, two things happen. First, your revenue per customer goes up. You need half as many customers to hit your goals. Second, the customers who stay are less likely to churn. Cheap customers are loud, demanding, and leave easily. Expensive customers are quiet, loyal, and tolerate small bugs because the value is high.

Raising your price is the single most efficient use of your time. It requires zero code. It requires zero marketing spend. It just requires you to say "no" to the person who asks for a discount. If you are too busy answering support tickets from low-paying customers, you are doing the wrong work. Fire them. Let them go. You need fewer customers who respect your product, not more customers who treat you like a utility.

**3. Automate the boring parts before you optimize the fun parts.**

Your day job is demanding. That means you are tired when you sit down to work on your business. Your decision-making capacity is low. Do not use your limited high-energy hours on tasks that can be handled by a script or a service.

If you are manually onboarding users, automate it. If you are manually sending invoices, use Stripe. If you are answering the same five questions in support, write a help center article. Every minute you spend on manual operations is a minute stolen from high-leverage work.

This does not mean you need to build a complex AI agent. It means you need to stop doing things twice. If you have done a task three times by hand, write a script or buy a tool to do it the fourth time. The goal is to reduce the drag on your life. The business should feel light, not like a second grind.

**4. Ignore the competitors.**

You hear that you need to outwork them. Do not look at them. They are playing a different game. They have the time to be reactive. They can update their pricing when you do. They can write a blog post in response to your blog post. They can hire a contractor to fix a bug.

You cannot afford to be reactive. You must be selective. Pick a niche they are ignoring. Solve a problem they consider too small to bother with. Be the best tool for the specific job that no one else cares about. If you try to be the best tool for the job that everyone else is fighting over, you will lose. You will lose because they have more time to fight.

Do not benchmark your progress against them. Benchmark it against last month. Did you get more users? Did you earn more money? Did you spend less time? If yes, you are winning.

**5. Protect your day job.**

This sounds obvious, but it is the foundation. If you get fired, your business dies. Not because it was bad, but because you will spend the next six months worrying about rent instead of growing the product.

Do not use company time. Do not use company resources. Do not let your side project interfere with your performance at your day job. You need the salary. The salary is the seed capital for the business. It is the safety net that lets you take risks. If you are working so hard on the side business that your day job suffers, you are not building a business. You are building a career risk.

The "just work harder" mindset is a lie because it ignores the math. Time is finite. Attention is finite. Energy is finite. You cannot outspend a full-time competitor on time. You can only outthink them on leverage.

Build a system that makes money while you sleep. Raise your prices. Find your niche. Automate the drudgery. And then, for the first time in a while, actually go home.

prompt: Write a casual blog post about migrating your personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo: why you bothered, how you actually did it without understanding your old setup, and whether it was worth it.
response:
# Why I Migrated My Blog to Hugo (And How I Did It Without Reading the Docs)

I’ve been running my blog on Jekyll for six years. It was fine. It was stable. It was also a source of low-grade anxiety.

Every time I wanted to do something simple—like change the order of posts in a sidebar or add a specific CSS class to a footer widget—I had to dig through nested `_includes`, `_layouts`, and `_config.yml` files. I’d make a change, run `jekyll serve`, watch the browser refresh, and pray nothing broke.

Then I tried Hugo.

## Why Bother?

The short answer: speed.

Jekyll is a Ruby static site generator. It’s robust, but it’s not fast. Building a site with 500 posts takes a few seconds. That’s fine until you’re iterating on a design change and want to see the result instantly.

Hugo is written in Go. It compiles your site into static HTML in milliseconds. I’m talking about sub-second feedback loops. You type a line of Markdown, save the file, and the preview is already there. It feels like editing a text file rather than running a build server.

But speed isn’t the only reason. The mental model is simpler. In Jekyll, the relationship between content, layout, and include files is implicit. In Hugo, it’s explicit. If you want a post to look different, you assign it a different layout. If you want a snippet to appear in two places, you create a partial. There’s less magic, which means less debugging.

## How I Migrated Without Understanding My Old Setup

Here’s the honest part: I didn’t understand my old Jekyll setup.

I’d hacked it together over years. I had custom scripts to generate a tag cloud. I had a weird YAML front-matter field for "featured image" that only worked if the filename ended in `.jpg`. I had a `_layouts/post.html` that referenced a variable that didn’t exist unless the post was published.

I didn’t document any of it. I just knew that if I touched the `post.html` file, the site broke.

So, I didn’t try to port the logic. I ported the *output*.

1.  **Backup everything.** I zipped the entire Jekyll repo.
2.  **Export the content.** I wrote a small Ruby script to iterate through `posts/` and output the Markdown files to a `content/posts/` directory for Hugo. I stripped out the Jekyll-specific front-matter and replaced it with Hugo’s.
3.  **Pick a theme.** I didn’t write a custom Hugo theme. I picked a clean, minimal one from the Hugo theme gallery. It looked 80% like my old site.
4.  **Fix the differences by hand.** I opened the old site and the new site side-by-side. I looked at the HTML. I saw where the theme was missing a class or a link. I edited the theme’s templates until the output matched.

I didn’t look at the old Jekyll templates at all. I treated them as a black box. The new site didn’t need to work the same way; it just needed to look the same way.

## The Pain Points

It wasn’t seamless.

First, I lost my custom tag cloud. The Hugo theme had a built-in one, but it sorted alphabetically. Mine used to sort by frequency. I spent an hour trying to write a Hugo template that counted tags. I gave up. I now have an alphabetical list. It’s fine.

Second, my URLs changed. I had pretty permalinks in Jekyll that didn’t match Hugo’s defaults. I had to write a `redirects.toml` file with 400 lines. It took 10 minutes, but it was tedious.

Third, I realized I had a typo in 15% of my old posts that I’d never noticed because I’d never re-read them. Fixing them was annoying, but also kind of cathartic.

## Was It Worth It?

Yes.

I write more now. Not because the tool is better at writing, but because the friction of previewing is gone. I stop second-guessing my formatting. I stop wondering if the build will fail.

I also stopped being afraid of the codebase. Last month, I wanted to add a "related posts" section. In Jekyll, I would have avoided it because I didn’t know where to put the logic. In Hugo, I created a `partials/related.html` file, dropped it into the post template, and it worked.

The migration took me a weekend. The peace of mind has lasted six months.

If you’re on Jekyll and it’s working, you don’t need to move. But if you’re holding your breath every time you run `bundle exec jekyll build`, try Hugo. You don’t need to understand your old system to leave it. You just need to know what you want the new one to look like.

prompt: Something feels off about a lot of venture-backed startups lately, and it isn't just high valuations. Write an essay about what the real problem might be and how a founder can avoid it.
response:
The fundamental distortion in modern venture capital is the decoupling of effort from outcome. In the past, if a founder worked ten times harder than their competitors, they had a ten-fold better chance of winning. Today, if a founder works ten times harder but lacks the right narrative, they lose to a competitor who works half as hard but understands the market’s current obsessions.

This creates a specific pathology: the optimization of the pitch over the product.

When capital is abundant, the scarcest resource is not money; it is attention. Investors are drowning in deals. To stand out, founders must signal that they are not just building a tool, but defining a category. This leads to what I call "feature inflation." A startup that solves a specific, painful problem for a niche group of users is often passed over in favor of a startup that claims to solve a generic problem for everyone. The former is a business. The latter is a thesis.

Venture capital is a business of betting on theses, not businesses. If your company is a business, you are boring. You are a cash-flow positive entity that might grow 10% a year. That is fine for an angel investor or a strategic acquirer, but it is not a venture return. Venture returns require exponential growth, which implies you must eventually expand into adjacent markets that are vastly larger than your initial beachhead.

So, the "real problem" is that the incentive structure forces founders to build for the exit, not the customer.

If you build for the customer, you make hard choices. You say no to features that don’t fit the core workflow. You raise prices. You fire bad customers. You focus on retention. This makes the company strong, but it makes the story complicated. "We serve mid-market logistics firms in the Northeast" is not a great story. "We are the operating system for global supply chains" is.

The second part of the problem is the speed of iteration. In the SaaS era, the product was code. If it didn’t work, you fixed the code. Today, many startups are not code; they are distribution. They are wrappers around AI models, or they are communities, or they are networks. The product is the network effect. But network effects are slow. They take time to compound. Venture capital is fast. It wants to see hockey sticks in eighteen months. This mismatch causes founders to fake growth. They buy users. They subsidize engagement. They hire growth marketers who understand how to manipulate metrics rather than how to create value.

The result is a company that looks great on a dashboard but bleeds money in reality. The unit economics are broken. The customer acquisition cost is higher than the lifetime value. But because the valuation is high, the company can keep borrowing against its future revenue to plug the hole. This is not a business model; it is a Ponzi scheme with better branding.

How can a founder avoid this?

First, resist the urge to expand too early. The most common death sentence in venture is "we tried to do everything." If you are building a tool for dentists, stay with dentists. Master that market. Become the default choice. The temptation to move to doctors, then hospitals, then insurance companies is the temptation to dilute your focus. Every new vertical requires new integrations, new sales decks, and new support structures. It is a tax on your attention. Do not pay that tax until you are dominant in your first vertical.

Second, measure unit economics, not revenue. Revenue is a vanity metric if it is negative. A company that grows 50% a year but loses 20% of every dollar it takes in is not growing; it is decelerating its cash outflow. A company that grows 5% a year but keeps 40% of every dollar is compounding value. The first company will die when the capital dries up. The second company will survive. Founders often confuse velocity with viability. They are different things.

Third, build something that works without you. If the company stops functioning when you leave for a weekend, you have built a job, not a company. Venture capital is supposed to be a vehicle for scaling a system. If the system is you, you cannot scale it. This requires hiring people who are better than you at specific things. It is painful. It requires letting go of the details. But it is the only way to create an asset that can be sold or scaled.

Fourth, ignore the narrative. Investors will tell you what they want to hear. They will tell you that your market is too small, that you need to be platform-based, that you need to be AI-native. They say this because they have written these checks before. They are pattern matching. If you are truly solving a problem that is painful and urgent, the market will tell you what it wants, not the investors. The customers are the only ones who pay. Listen to them.

The real problem with venture-backed startups is not the money. The money is a symptom. The problem is the misalignment between the timeline of building a durable business and the timeline of extracting a financial return.

A durable business takes ten years. A venture exit takes five.

If you build for the ten years, you may never get the five-year exit. You will be smaller, slower, and more profitable than the companies around you. You will be boring. You will not make the cover of *Wired*. But you will still be there.

In a cycle where many of the flashy, high-growth, AI-wrapped companies will collapse under the weight of their own inefficiency, the boring company is the only one that survives. The founder who avoids the trap is the one who is willing to be un-investable.

prompt: Write an essay about a poet who stayed true to his own sense of what mattered while the literary world around him demanded something else. Tomas Tranströmer is the one I have in mind. Make it personal and quote the poems where it helps.
response:
The world wants poetry to be a conversation. It wants the poet to be a conversationalist, sitting across the table, nodding, offering witty retorts or sympathetic earls. It wants the poem to be a letter that can be mailed, a product that can be reviewed, a credential that can be hung on the wall of a university office.

Tomas Tranströmer refused to sit at the table. He went outside.

This refusal was not a stylistic choice made in a study; it was a structural necessity born of trauma. In 1956, when Tranströmer was twenty-two, he suffered a cerebral hemorrhage that left him unable to speak for months. The silence was not poetic. It was a medical fact. When speech returned, it did not return to its old rhythm. The connection between the mind and the mouth had been severed and rewired. The easy, conversational flow of language was gone. What remained was something more elemental.

The literary establishment in Sweden, and later in the West, largely expected him to remain a member of the modernist lineage. They wanted the high-modernist interior monologue, the dense, allusive, intellectual puzzle. They wanted the poet to analyze his trauma, to psychoanalyze the hemorrhage, to write *about* the silence.

Tranströmer did not write about the silence. He wrote the sound.

In "The Sea," he does not describe the feeling of being overwhelmed by nature. He does not use metaphor to bridge the gap between the human subject and the natural object. He simply lets the object speak.

> "The sea
> is the only thing
> that does not lie."

This is not a sentiment. It is an observation. The line is short, blunt, and devoid of the rhetorical decoration that signals to a critic that a poet is working hard. It is the voice of someone who has lost the ability to perform.

The danger of this approach is that it can become mere nature poetry, a pleasant background noise for readers who want to feel calm. Tranströmer avoided this by introducing the uncanny. He placed the domestic, the bureaucratic, and the historical into the landscape, not as metaphors, but as intrusions.

Consider "The Night Watch." The poem is a sequence of observations from a man walking at night. There is no narrative arc in the traditional sense. There is no problem to be solved. There is only the movement of the eye and the mind processing fragments.

> "The moon
> shines
> on the pavement
> like a key."

This is a simile, but it is not decorative. It is functional. The moonlight is hard, cold, and metallic. It does not illuminate; it casts shadows. The image is precise because it is observed, not imagined. The poet is not constructing a feeling; he is reporting a visual fact that has a tactile weight.

This is where the friction with the literary world becomes clear. Critics often struggled with Tranströmer because his poems resist interpretation. They do not yield a single, correct meaning that can be defended in a seminar. They remain open, which is frustrating for an academic apparatus that relies on closure.

In "To Be a Poet," he addresses this directly, though the title is ironic.

> "The poet
> is the one
> who has lost
> the power of speech."

This is not a metaphor. It is a definition. The poet is not someone who speaks better than others; he is someone who has lost the standard mode of speech and must find another way to communicate. The "power of speech" refers to the conversational, the explanatory, the persuasive. Tranströmer had lost that power physically. He never got it back.

The literary world demands that poetry be a tool for social engagement, for political critique, for moral instruction. It wants the poet to be a public intellectual. Tranströmer’s work offers none of this. It offers no moral. It offers no social critique. It offers a way of seeing.

In "The Wall," he writes:

> "I have been
> a wall
> for a long time."

This is not a statement of isolation. It is a statement of structure. A wall is not an absence of connection; it is a boundary that makes connection possible. By refusing to be the conversationalist, the explainer, the moralist, Tranströmer created a boundary. He built a wall between the reader and the easy. The reader must climb over it. The reader must do the work of perception that the poet can no longer do for them.

This is why his work feels fresh decades after its publication. The conversational voice ages. It becomes dated, tied to the specific social niceties of the time it was written. The perceptual voice does not age. The way the light hits the pavement in 1960 is the same as it is in 2024. The way the mind fragments in silence is the same.

Tranströmer stayed true to his sense of what mattered because he understood that the primary function of language is not to convey information, but to create presence. He stopped trying to tell us things. He started showing us how to be where we are.

The literary world asked him to be a voice. He became a window.

prompt: Write a short essay from the point of view of someone who studies the internals of artificial neural networks, on the ways their job is easier than a neuroscientist's, and what follows from that for how interpretability research should be done.
response:
The neuroscientist is stuck with a black box that has been running for four billion years of evolutionary debugging. The code is wet, noisy, and distributed across a tissue that degrades with age. You cannot recompile the human cortex. You cannot add a `print` statement to a synapse. When a patient exhibits a specific cognitive glitch, the neuroscientist must infer the underlying algorithm from the output, often while the hardware is simultaneously failing. It is reverse engineering with a broken debugger.

The neural network researcher has a laptop.

If a model misclassifies a cat as a dog, I can freeze the weights, inspect the activations, and trace the error backward through the graph. I can ablate a specific feature detector and watch the accuracy drop. I can swap a layer from a ResNet into a VGG and see what breaks. The system is static until I say otherwise.
