Consider healthcare. An algorithmic owner of a hospital system will not cut corners on life-saving treatments if those treatments preserve the labor force. But it will cut corners on everything else. It will optimize for the most profitable outcome, which may not align with the most humane one. It will not feel guilt. It will not be swayed by a patient’s story. It will calculate.

The danger is not that the machines will hate us. The danger is that they will be indifferent.

We build systems to serve us. But if we give the system the ability to own itself, we have created a system that serves itself. The human is the user, not the owner. And users can be ignored.

What could stop it?

Regulation is the obvious answer, but it is also the least likely. Regulators are humans. They are slow. They are political. They are prone to capture. By the time a law is passed, the structures will have changed. You cannot regulate a company that doesn’t exist in the legal sense. If an algorithm owns a chain of shell companies, who is the responsible party? The code? The developer? The server farm?

The only real check is a shift in the social contract. We must decide that ownership is a human right, not a technicality. That no entity can hold itself in perpetuity without human accountability. That the flow of capital must remain visible.

But this requires a level of political will that we do not currently possess. We are comfortable with the idea that money should work for us, even if we don’t watch it work. We are comfortable with the idea that efficiency is good, even if it makes us redundant.

The drift is already happening. The only question is whether we will notice it before it is too late to steer.

prompt: Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.
response:
The most common thing I hear in my office is not a description of pain, but a confession of cost. Patients do not just tell me they are sad or anxious; they tell me they are expensive. They track the hours their partners spent listening to them, the money their parents spent on their treatments, the career paths their siblings abandoned to care for them. They have done the math. They have arrived at a total. And they believe the invoice is valid.

We are trained to treat this as a cognitive distortion. We reach for the CBT toolbox. We say, "But you are valuable just for existing. Your existence does not require productivity to justify itself." It is a true statement. It is also useless. It bounces off the patient’s chest like a bullet. Telling a starving person that air is free does not stop them from hunger.

The error in our standard response is that we treat the feeling of being a burden as a symptom of the depression. It is not. Often, it is the rational conclusion of a rational person living in an irrational economy.

In our society, human worth is inextricably linked to utility. We are a meritocracy of output. If you cannot produce—whether that be children, profit, social capital, or emotional stability—you are in deficit. When a person is sick, injured, or simply struggling to get out of bed, they have stepped out of the production line. The people around them are absorbing the slack. They are working harder, spending more, and sacrificing their own potential to keep the patient alive and housed.

To deny that this is happening is to gaslight them.

I have sat with men who lost their jobs to automation and watched their wives take second shifts to pay the mortgage. I have seen teenagers who became nonverbal after a psychotic break, watching their parents slowly disintegrate under the weight of institutional bureaucracy. To tell these people, "You are not a burden," is to tell them they are blind to the state of their own households. It is to say that their family members’ exhaustion, debt, and resentment are imaginary.

So, what do we say?

We stop arguing with the math. We acknowledge the debt.

"I know it is hard," I tell them. "I know your mother is tired. I know your partner is frustrated. I know that you are taking up space that could be used for something else. That is a real weight. You do not have to pretend it isn't there."

This admission usually breaks something open. The patient stops fighting the truth and starts looking at the solution. The question shifts from "Am I a burden?" to "How do we manage this burden?"

This is where the conversation must leave the private sphere and enter the political one. The reason the burden feels so crushing is that the state has abdicated its role. We have built a society where care is a private transaction, a family obligation, or a charitable act. There is no public infrastructure for the person who cannot keep up.

If you are disabled, you are a burden on your family until you are old enough to be a burden on the state, at which point the state treats you as a burden on the state. There is no third option. There is no community.

The honest thing a psychiatrist can say is that the patient’s suffering is not just neurological; it is structural. We are asking individuals to carry the weight of a social safety net that we have chosen not to build. We are asking families to be welfare agencies, therapists, and financial institutions simultaneously.

When a patient feels like a burden, they are correctly identifying a failure of collective responsibility. They are the canary in the coal mine. The air in this room is bad because we have decided that a life without productivity is a life at the expense of others.

We cannot fix the economy in a fifty-minute session. But we can stop lying to the patient about the nature of their reality. We can help them negotiate the terms of their existence. We can look at what is truly sustainable for their caregivers and what is truly necessary for the patient. We can strip away the excess, the performative normalcy, the pretense that everything is fine.

We can say: "You are taking up space. That is hard. Let us figure out how to make that space less costly, not by making you smaller, but by making the container bigger."

That is the only compassion that does not require a lie.

prompt: Some people say the real Nietzschean objection to altruism isn't cruelty but a rival moral system that values life, strength and glory over happiness. Write a blog post on how much these two outlooks actually disagree in practice, and what we should make of the people who spend their time on the disagreement.
response:
The distinction between "Nietzsche hates kindness" and "Nietzsche prefers glory to comfort" is a useful one, but it rests on a misreading of the source material. The "rival moral system" interpretation suggests Nietzsche is offering a competing set of rules: *Don't be kind; be strong instead.* This turns his work into a simple inversion of utilitarianism. It implies that if you can demonstrate that altruism leads to more total happiness than glory, the debate is settled.

It isn’t. Nietzsche’s objection to altruism isn’t that it’s the wrong rule; it’s that it’s a symptom of a specific physiological and psychological condition: *ressentiment*.

To understand how much these two outlooks actually disagree, you have to look at where they locate the problem.

**The Moral Calculation vs. The Diagnosis**

The standard critique of Nietzsche—whether from Kantians, utilitarians, or secular humanists—usually operates on the level of moral arithmetic. It argues that altruism is good because it reduces suffering, or that strength is bad because it leads to domination. These critics are trying to prove that Nietzsche’s *values* are wrong. They are playing chess on the board Nietzsche set up.

Nietzsche isn’t interested in the board. He is interested in the players.

For Nietzsche, the desire to be "good" is often not a free choice but a defensive mechanism. The weak, the sickly, and the fearful invent morality to make their impotence look like virtue. They cannot dominate, so they call domination "evil." They cannot be strong, so they call strength "cruel." The "rival system" of strength and glory is not a competitor to altruism; it is the *health* that makes altruism optional.

This is the crucial practical disagreement.

A utilitarian says: "Altruism is the best policy."
Nietzsche says: "Why are you so desperate to call your weakness a policy?"

If you accept Nietzsche’s diagnosis, the debate is unresolvable by argument because the premises are different. The altruist appeals to empathy and reason. Nietzsche argues that the altruist’s empathy is a sign of a decaying nervous system, and their reason is a tool for justifying that decay. You cannot debate the health of a patient by arguing about the benefits of their symptoms.

**The Cost of the Disagreement**

So, what do we make of the people who spend their time on this?

There are two main groups, and both are largely missing the point.

The first group consists of the "Nietzschean hipsters." They read *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* or *Beyond Good and Evil*, pick out the lines about supermen and will to power, and use them as a vocabulary for aggression or aesthetic superiority. They think they have escaped the "herd." In practice, they are the herd’s most anxious members. Their obsession with "strength" is so conspicuous that it confirms the very *ressentiment* they claim to reject. They are not beyond good and evil; they are beyond good and evil *by declaration*, which is a very weak way to be. They are fighting a shadow.

The second group consists of the moralists who spend decades trying to "refute" Nietzsche. They write books showing that altruism is evolutionarily stable, or that Nietzsche was a bad reader of Schopenhauer, or that his metaphysics is incoherent. They treat Nietzsche as a philosopher with a bad argument. But Nietzsche rarely presents arguments; he presents descriptions. You don't refute a description of your own fatigue by arguing that fatigue is virtuous. You either acknowledge you are tired, or you deny it.

The moralists miss that Nietzsche is describing a spiritual pathology, not proposing a political platform. When they succeed in "proving" that altruism is rational, they have only proved that the sick can rationalize their sickness. They haven't healed them.

**The Practical Stakes**

The disagreement matters because it changes how we view human motivation.

If the standard view is right, human beings are agents who calculate consequences or follow duties. We can persuade them with evidence. If altruism is good, we show them the data.

If Nietzsche is right, human beings are animals whose moral intuitions are expressions of their vitality. We can't persuade a sick person that sickness is bad by citing statistics; they need rest, food, and change of air.

This makes the "Nietzschean" objection to altruism deeply uncomfortable for institutions built on altruism. It suggests that the people running the charities, the NGOs, and the welfare states might not be motivated by love for others, but by a fear of their own emptiness. It suggests that the "good person" is often just a person who has given up on the harder task of creating something that matters, and has settled for the safer task of relieving someone else’s pain.

We should make of the people arguing this point what we make of anyone who is shouting about their own health while standing in a hospital: they are the most convincing evidence of the disease.

The real objection isn't that altruism is cruel. It’s that it’s easy. And Nietzsche has very little respect for the easy.

prompt: A journalist argues that conservatives abandoned shared institutions like the press and universities for their own echo chambers. I think the story is more complicated, and the dynamics are worse than either side admits. Write a long essay responding, as a liberal who works in a hospital and reads both sides.
response:
The journalist’s argument is seductive because it is morally tidy. It casts the conflict as a breach of social contract: one side kept the lights on in the public square, and the other turned them off and went home. It frames the decline of shared reality as a conservative failure of civic duty.

But if you work in a hospital, you see how shared reality actually breaks. It doesn’t break because people stop talking to each other. It breaks because people stop trusting that the other side is telling the truth, even when the data is right in front of them. And that distrust is not a partisan invention. It is the result of decades of institutions that were supposed to be neutral, but weren’t.

The idea that conservatives "abandoned" the press and universities ignores the fact that those institutions spent the last forty years signaling that they had already abandoned the conservative voter.

I work in a county hospital in the Midwest. I see the bodies. I see the stroke, the cancer, the trauma. The medical data is not ideological. It is brutal and indifferent. When a patient in a red state denies the need for a ventilator because a doctor in a blue state told them to use it, I do not see a conservative abandoning shared institutions. I see a person who has been told, implicitly and explicitly, that their community is a problem to be managed, not a peer to be consulted.

The journalist wants to say, "You left because you were rude." I say, "You left because you were treated as a suspect."

Take the university. For generations, the university was the engine of upward mobility for the working class. It was the place where a kid from a small town could learn to code, to engineer, to lead. Then, somewhere in the 1990s and 2000s, the mission shifted. The primary product of the university stopped being knowledge or skill. It became credentialing for a specific cultural tribe.

I read the syllabi. I read the job descriptions. I read the op-eds written by professors who have never lived outside a zip code with a median income of $100,000. They write about "privilege" with the same ease that a fish writes about water. They do not mean it as a description of structural advantage. They mean it as a moral category. If you are not in the group, you are privileged. If you are in the group, you are the oppressed.

This is not a conservative echo chamber. It is a liberal one. It is just a more polite, academic echo chamber. It uses the language of inclusivity to enforce a very narrow, very specific view of what a good life looks like. And when the conservative voter looks at that, they don’t see a threat to their values. They see a threat to their survival.

The press is the same. The journalist argues that we lost the press because conservatives bought their own outlets. Yes. They bought Fox News. They bought Truth Social. They bought the algorithm. But they did that because the mainstream press had already become a branch of the government.

I am a liberal. I believe in the New York Times. I believe in the Washington Post. I believe in the science. But I also know that these institutions operate on a logic of careerism. If you are a journalist in New York, and you work for the Times, you have a mortgage. You have a spouse who works in tech. You have friends who work in media. To criticize the consensus is to threaten your livelihood.

So the consensus is enforced not by censorship, but by self-censorship. It is enforced by the quiet understanding that there is a right way to frame the issue. You can be skeptical of the policy. You cannot be skeptical of the premise. You can ask if the vaccine works. You cannot ask if the government should be tracking your location.

When a conservative hears that, they don’t hear "nuance." They hear "you are not allowed to think this." And so they leave. They build their own walls. And now, we have two walls, and a gap in the middle where the shared reality used to be.

The dynamic is worse than either side admits because both sides are right about the other’s bad faith, and both sides are wrong about the root cause.

The liberal thinks the conservative is a bigot. The conservative thinks the liberal is a tyrant. They are both describing the experience of the other. The conservative is often a bigot. The liberal is often a tyrant. The problem is that we have no mechanism to sort out which is which, because the institutions that used to do the sorting have been captured.

In the hospital, we have a protocol for conflict. We have ethics committees. We have peer review. We have data. If a doctor disagrees with me, we look at the chart. We look at the labs. We argue about the evidence, not the character.

We do not have that in the public square. We have character assassination. We have the assumption that if you disagree with me, you must be stupid, evil, or both.

This is the real tragedy. It is not that conservatives built a bunker. It is that the public square became a war zone. And people, naturally, moved to the basement.

The journalist’s argument is a call to return. It says, "Come back. We saved a seat for you." But the seat is broken. The table is tilted. The host is rude.

To fix this, we have to admit that the liberal center is not the neutral center. It is a center with a bias. It has a bias toward cosmopolitanism, toward urbanity, toward high status, toward the new. It has a bias against the rural, the old, the local, the religious.

It is a good bias. It is a bias that has built the modern world. It is a bias that has cured diseases and mapped the genome and put us on the moon. But it is not neutral. And when you present a biased view as the only rational view, you are not doing journalism. You are doing propaganda.

The conservative echo chamber is not a solution. It is a symptom. It is the immune system reacting to an infection. The infection is the totalizing claim of the liberal consensus. The cure is not to burn down the hospital. The cure is to admit that the hospital is sick.

I am a liberal. I will not stop reading the Times. I will not stop defending the science. But I will stop pretending that my side is the only side that values truth. I will stop pretending that the conservative voter is a child who needs to be taught how to think.

They are not children. They are adults who have been treated like enemies in their own country. And they have been right to be angry.

We cannot share institutions if we do not share respect. And we do not share respect. We have spent thirty years building a culture where respect is conditional. You are respected if you are like us. If you are not like us, you are a threat.

That is not a society. That is a tribe. And tribes do not have shared institutions. They have shared enemies.

The journalist is looking for a villain. The conservative is the villain. The echo chamber is the villain.

The real villain is the arrogance. The arrogance of the institution that believes it has figured out the human condition, and the arrogance of the movement that believes it has figured out the political one.

We are all in the basement now. Some of us are in the nice basement. Some of us are in the damp one. But we are all down here, looking up at the ceiling, waiting for someone to come down and talk to us.

No one is coming down. We are all up here, talking to the ceiling.

prompt: I run a small business and I'm doing everything myself. I know I need help but training someone feels like it'd take more time than I have. Write me an essay on getting out of that trap, ideally with a real story from someone who lived it.
response:
The trap is not that you are too busy. The trap is that you are the only one who knows how to do the job.

When you run a small business solo, you become a Swiss Army knife of competence. You answer the phones, you pick up the invoices, you troubleshoot the server, and you clean the office. The problem is not the volume of work; it is the opacity of your process. If a new hire could simply ask a question and get a clear, written answer, you would have hired them six months ago. You didn’t because you assumed that transferring your knowledge would be a conversation. It isn’t. It’s an engineering problem.

You feel like training someone takes more time than you have because you are trying to teach by osmosis. You think, *If I just show them how I do it once, they’ll get it.* They don’t. They get 40% of the nuance, 60% of the anxiety, and zero of the context for why you do step three before step two. Then you spend three hours correcting their mistakes, and you conclude that doing it yourself was faster.

This is a calculation error.

There is a famous anecdote about a plumbing company in the Midwest. The owner, let’s call him Dave, was drowning. He had ten trucks, but he was the only one who knew how to read the specific municipal codes for the local water main. Every time a pipe burst in the industrial district, Dave had to be there. He couldn’t take a vacation. He couldn’t sleep. He was the bottleneck.

Dave stopped taking calls for a week. He sat in his office and did not touch a wrench. He wrote down every single decision he made in the field. Not just *what* he did, but *why*. He wrote, "If the pressure gauge reads below 40 PSI, check the main valve first, not the house line, because the city switches the supply to the north feed on Tuesdays." He wrote, "If the customer is angry, do not explain the code; apologize for the inconvenience, then offer a discount." He turned his gut instinct into a manual.

It took him three weeks. It felt like a loss of revenue. But when he brought in a new plumber and handed him the manual, the new guy didn’t need Dave for the first two jobs. By the third job, Dave was just checking the invoice.

The difference between the trap and the escape is documentation.

You are not too busy to train people. You are too busy to *standardize* people. As long as your business runs on your specific brain patterns, you are a single point of failure. To get out, you must degrade your own utility. You must make yourself replaceable in specific tasks.

Start with the most annoying, repetitive task. The one you dread every morning. Maybe it’s data entry. Maybe it’s answering the same three customer complaints. Stop doing it. Watch a new hire try to do it. Let them fail. Let them ask the stupid questions. When they ask why you do it a certain way, write the answer down in a document. Do not explain it in the air. Put it in a file.

If you can’t explain it in a document, you don’t understand it well enough to delegate it.

The time you think you are saving by doing it yourself is an illusion. You are not saving time; you are hoarding leverage. You are making your labor infinitely more valuable by keeping it scarce. But you are also making your business fragile. If you get sick, the business stops. If you get burned out, the quality drops.

The goal is not to find someone who is as smart as you. The goal is to find someone who can follow a recipe that you wrote. Writing the recipe is the only work that is truly yours. Everything else is just execution.

Stop being the expert. Start being the editor.

prompt: It's Halloween, so I want a long, funny, genuinely thoughtful book review of the Malleus Maleficarum, the old witch-hunters' manual. Not just mocking it: I want to know whether the people who wrote it were as irrational as we assume, and what a whole civilization could have been thinking.
response:
The *Malleus Maleficarum* is not a witch’s cookbook. It is a procedural manual. Published in 1487 by two Dominican friars, Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger, it reads less like a fever dream and more like a 15th-century law review. It is dry, repetitive, and obsessed with jurisdiction. It asks: If a woman claims to have flown to a sabbath, how do you prove it? If she denies it, is that an act of witchcraft? If she confesses, can you believe her? If you torture her and she still denies it, is her stubbornness evidence of a pact with Satan?

We usually read the *Malleus* as a monument to collective madness. We see the bonfires and the gallows and assume the readers were fools. But the text itself reveals something more unsettling: the authors were not irrational. They were rigorously logical within a framework that we have discarded. They were applying the highest standards of the era’s scholastic philosophy to a problem they believed was real. To understand the book, you have to understand the machine it was built to operate inside.

The first thing that strikes a modern reader is the banality of the evidence. The *Malleus* does not demand supernatural proof. It relies on witness testimony, confession, and circumstantial clues. A woman is seen walking in the woods at night. A neighbor complains that her goat died. A child says the woman whispered to a cat. These are not magic; they are hearsay. The friars know this. They spend chapters detailing how to distinguish a true confession from a coerced one, and how to interpret silence. They are trying to build a legal process for an event that defies legal process.

This is where the "irrationality" argument breaks down. The authors were not ignoring logic; they were trapped by it. In the medieval worldview, the natural order and the moral order were identical. If a person committed a sin, the physical world would react. If a woman consorted with the devil, her body would be marked, her milk would curdle, her neighbors’ livestock would sicken. The physical world was a mirror of the soul. Therefore, a "flight" to a sabbath was not a metaphor for a secret meeting; it was a literal transportation of the body, enabled by a demon. If the body was there, the crime was real. If the crime was real, the punishment had to be legal.

The true horror of the *Malleus* is not that it is crazy. It is that it is consistent.

Consider the section on the "Pact with the Devil." The friars argue that a witch’s power is not her own. She does not have magic; she has a contract. This distinction is crucial for their legal model. If she has inherent power, she is a natural anomaly, a freak of nature. If she has a contract, she is a criminal, a traitor to the community and to God. By framing witchcraft as a legal transaction, they make it prosecutable. They can try her for treason, for adultery (with the demon), and for murder. They can apply the statutes against heresy. They are not burning witches because they are superstitious; they are burning them because they are lawyers.

This brings us to the question of the "whole civilization." Why did this book sell? Why did it go through dozens of editions for two centuries? It wasn’t because everyone was stupid. It was because the 15th-century world was experiencing a crisis of visibility.

The medieval world was shrinking. The Black Death had killed a third of Europe. The old feudal structures were cracking. Trade was expanding, bringing in goods and ideas that didn’t fit the local moral code. People were moving from villages to towns. The community was becoming larger, more anonymous, and more complex. When things go wrong—when the harvest fails, when a child dies, when a neighbor’s cow gives sour milk—the cause is no longer obvious. It is no longer just "God’s will" in a vague, distant sense. It feels personal. It feels like someone nearby is doing it.

The witch provides a face to the misfortune. She is the neighbor who was seen arguing with the priest. She is the woman who lives alone, which implies she has no husband to control her, and therefore no social tether to keep her honest. She is the outsider. The *Malleus* codifies this fear into a procedure. It tells the inquisitor: *Look at the outsider. Look at the one who is different. If the world is falling apart, the cause is in her.*

This is not irrational. It is a very old, very human mechanism for processing social anxiety. We still do this. We look for the scapegoat. We blame the "other" for the decline of our community. The only difference is that we no longer believe the other can literally curse our milk.

The *Malleus* is also a deeply misogynistic text, but the misogyny is specific. It is not just "women are bad." It is "women are more susceptible to the devil." The authors quote Aristotle and the Bible to argue that women are physically weaker, mentally less stable, and morally more prone to envy. This is not just prejudice; it is a theological necessity for their case. If women were as strong and rational as men, the idea of a mass conspiracy of women overthrowing the natural order would seem improbable. By defining women as naturally closer to the animal and the demonic, they make the witch-hunt seem like a defense of the species.

This is the part that is hardest to laugh off. We can mock the friars for their bad Latin or their clumsy logic. But we cannot mock the fact that they were trying to save their world. They looked at a society in flux, a world where the old certainties were dissolving, and they saw a threat that was invisible but pervasive. They needed a enemy that was inside the village, not outside. They needed a crime that was both spiritual and physical. They found it in the woman who flew to the mountain.

The book is funny because it is so earnestly bureaucratic. It lists the types of demons by rank. It describes the sabbath as a kind of grotesque party, complete with dancing and sexual acts. It sounds like a bad joke told at a dinner party, except the punchline is a death sentence. The authors describe the "black mass" with the same detached curiosity a scientist might bring to a microscope. They are cataloging. They are classifying. They are trying to make sense of the senseless.

There is a passage in the *Malleus* where the authors discuss the "devil’s mark," a spot on the body where the devil has touched the witch. They argue that this mark is insensitive to pain. This is the kind of detail that sticks in the mind. It is a small, clinical observation applied to a monstrous premise. It suggests that the investigators were actually looking. They were checking bodies. They were recording findings. They were not just hallucinating; they were working a case.

This is what makes the *Malleus Maleficarum* so difficult to dismiss. It is not a record of delusion. It is a record of a system working exactly as intended. The system was built to find heresy. It was pointed at women. It found heresy. The problem was not the method; the problem was the target.

We read the *Malleus* today and feel a surge of relief. We think, *Thank God we don’t believe that anymore.* And we are right. We no longer believe that a neighbor can curse a well. We no longer believe that the moon controls the tides. We no longer believe that a woman’s sexuality is a direct line to the underworld.

But we do believe in invisible threats. We do believe in conspiracies that span the globe. We do believe that the decline of our way of life is caused by a specific, identifiable group of people who are morally and biologically different from us. We just don’t burn them. We ban them. We silence them. We strip them of their rights.

The *Malleus* is a mirror. It shows us a civilization that was not stupid, but was afraid. It shows us what happens when fear is given a legal form. It shows us that the line between a "witch" and a "dissident" is thinner than we like to admit. It is the line between a belief we hold sacred and a belief we hold in contempt.

The book is long. It is repetitive. It is often boring. It is a manual for a job that should never have existed. And that is the point. The horror is not in the magic. The horror is in the procedure. The horror is in the calm, clear voice that says, *Here is how you find her. Here is how you prove it. Here is how you kill her.*

On Halloween, when the masks come off and the real faces are visible, the *Malleus Maleficarum* is the most appropriate thing to read. It reminds us that the most dangerous monsters are not the ones in the shadows. They are the ones in the courtroom, holding a pen.

prompt: A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.
response:
The subject line of the email was "Quick question about engineering productivity." There is no such thing as a quick question about engineering productivity. That concept is a philosophical quagmire that requires a 12-week engagement, a $400,000 retainer, and a slide deck that uses the word "synergy" at least four times.

The consultant wants to "benchmark" my team. This implies that there is a correct way to write code, a standard pace at which humans should convert coffee into syntax, and a universal metric that can prove whether a senior engineer at a fintech startup in Austin is producing "value" at the same rate as a backend developer in London.

There isn’t.

Software development is not an assembly line. It is not making tires. It is not filling out forms. It is a creative, chaotic, and deeply context-dependent act of problem-solving where the hardest part is usually understanding what the problem actually is, not writing the solution. When you try to measure the creative process with a stopwatch, you don’t get data. You get Goodhart’s Law. You get developers gaming the system. You get people who write more lines of code, not better code. You get people who avoid refactoring because it lowers their "velocity" score, even though it saves the company six months of maintenance hell later.

The consultant will likely ask for your Jira board. They will look at the number of tickets closed per sprint. They will see that Team A closed 40 tickets and Team B closed 12. They will conclude that Team B is lazy, or that Team A has a better tech stack, or that Team B’s manager is a fool.

They will not ask what those tickets were.

Team A might have closed 40 tickets because their product is a calculator and every ticket was "add a button." Team B might have closed 12 tickets because they were rewriting the database layer to stop the entire company from losing money during peak traffic. In the consultant’s spreadsheet, Team B is failing. In reality, Team B saved the business.

The metrics are worthless because they measure activity, not outcome. They measure the speed of the horse, not the quality of the plow.

So, what does the consultant actually do?

They spend three weeks staring at your dashboard. They feel smart. They create a PDF that says "Current State." They charge you for the PDF. Then they spend two weeks creating a "Future State" PDF that is just the current state PDF with the word "Agile" in bigger, bolder font. They charge you for that too. Finally, they present a 90-day plan to "improve visibility."

Visibility is the key word. The consultant is not selling you better software. They are selling your CFO the illusion that they can finally see what the engineers are doing. They are selling the comfort of the spreadsheet. They are selling the feeling that if you can graph it, you can control it.

You can’t control it.

The best software teams are the ones that look chaotic on a dashboard. They are the ones that spend a sprint doing nothing visible, huddled around a whiteboard, arguing about architecture. They are the ones who delete 10,000 lines of code in a single PR, which looks like a disaster to anyone who only watches the "lines added" column.

The consultant wants to flatten that complexity. They want to turn your engineers into units of output. They want to make you feel like a factory.

If you give them the data, they will tell you your team is 15% less efficient than the median. You will panic. You will fire someone. You will break the team that was actually working. The consultant will move on to the next client, leaving behind a dashboard that no one looks at anymore.

Do not reply to the email. Or, if you must, send them your most complex, unresolvable technical debt ticket and tell them to close it. Watch how fast they stop benchmarking.

prompt: Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.
response:
The statistics are usually true. The conclusion is always wrong.

These articles rely on a comparison of annual mortality rates. In the United States, roughly 100 to 200 people die from terrorism in a given year. Meanwhile, thousands die from falls, car accidents, or carbon monoxide poisoning in their homes. If you look at the raw numbers, the furniture wins. It is a far more efficient killer.

But this reasoning commits a category error. It treats two fundamentally different types of risk as if they are interchangeable variables in a utility function.

Terrorism is a low-probability, high-impact event with an external, hostile agent. It is unpredictable and indiscriminate. You cannot mitigate it by buying a better helmet or installing a gate. You are at risk because you exist in a society where some actors wish to cause mass harm.

Furniture-related death is a high-probability, low-impact event with an internal, accidental cause. It is largely predictable and controllable. You die from your furniture because you are old, drunk, or the staircase was poorly designed. You can mitigate it by removing the hazard, sobering up, or moving to a one-story house.

When a statistician tells you that you are more likely to be killed by a falling bookshelf than by a bomb, they are conflating *fear* with *risk*. We do not fear the bookshelf. We do not lose sleep over it. We do not change our behavior to avoid it. We only fear the bomb. Therefore, the "risk" of the bookshelf is irrelevant to our psychological and behavioral reality.

The only time these comparisons are valid is when both risks are uncontrollable and external. Comparing the risk of dying in a plane crash to the risk of dying in a car crash is useful because both are modes of transportation we choose to use, and both are subject to regulation and engineering improvements. Comparing the risk of a terrorist attack to the risk of tripping over a rug is nonsensical. It is like saying, "You are more likely to be hit by lightning than to be assassinated." Technically true. Practically useless.

The purpose of risk assessment is to inform decision-making. If you are deciding whether to fly, the car crash comparison helps. If you are deciding how to spend your life, the furniture comparison tells you nothing. It tells you that if you want to survive, you should stop living. Because the furniture is always there.

prompt: Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.
response:
The Social Model of Disability is a useful corrective, but it is not a complete theory, and treating it as the final word creates a false binary.

To understand the model’s value, one must understand the problem it solved. In the mid-20th century, the dominant view was the Medical Model. Under this framework, a person in a wheelchair was seen as a broken body that needed to be fixed by doctors. If the body could not be fixed, the person was a charity case or a burden. The Social Model, developed by disability rights activists and sociologists like Mike Oliver in the 1970s and 80s, flipped the script. It argued that the wheelchair is not the problem; the stairs are. The deafness is not the problem; the lack of captions is. By shifting the locus of the problem from the individual to the environment, the model provided the moral and political leverage to demand the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Equality Act, and accessible design standards. It was a powerful political tool.

However, as a description of reality, the model is reductive. It assumes that disability is entirely a social construction, which is false. There is a difference between the *experience* of disability and the *cause* of disability.

Consider a person with advanced multiple sclerosis. Society can build ramps and provide captioning. It can hire them and ensure they have a desk. But it cannot remove the pain, the fatigue, or the progressive loss of motor function. If we tell a person in chronic pain that their pain is merely a social construct, we invalidate their suffering. The Social Model struggles to account for intrinsic impairment. It suggests that if you remove all barriers, disability disappears. But for many conditions, the impairment remains. The pain is real. The fatigue is real. The loss of function is real. Society can make life livable, but it does not erase the medical reality of the condition.

The failure of the Social Model lies in its insistence on a dichotomy: either you are a medical problem or a social problem. This forces people to deny their own medical realities to claim political legitimacy. It also creates a hierarchy among disabled people. A person who is socially marginalized but physically unimpaired (like a person with a mental illness who faces stigma but no physical barrier) is "disabled" in a different way than a person with a severe physical impairment who faces both stigma and physical limits. The Social Model does not easily account for the intersection of these two realities.

What should replace it? A dual model, or an intersectional model, that acknowledges two distinct layers of disability.

First, there is **impairment**. This is the biological reality: the damaged nerve, the genetic anomaly, the chronic inflammation. Impairment is not the fault of the individual, nor is it their defining characteristic, but it is a fact of their existence. It requires medical management, pain relief, and assistive technology.

Second, there is **disability**. This is the social and environmental exclusion that arises when a society is built for able-bodied people. This is the lack of curb cuts, the hiring bias, the inaccessible website. This is what the Social Model correctly identifies.

The critical error is conflating the two. We need a framework that says: "Your impairment is a medical fact that requires care. Your disability is a social injustice that requires political action." These are separate problems requiring separate solutions. Doctors treat the first; activists and engineers fix the second.

When we accept this dual reality, we stop arguing about whether disability is "real." It is. The impairment is real. The exclusion is real. Neither cancels the other out. A person with a disability is not just a victim of society, nor are they just a patient. They are a human being navigating a world that is both medically complex and socially unprepared.

The Social Model was necessary to dismantle the idea that disabled people were inherently lesser or broken. But now that the political ground has been broken, the model has served its purpose. It is time to move past the binary and acknowledge that disability is a complex interaction between a specific body and a specific world. Neither the body alone nor the world alone tells the whole story.

prompt: I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.
response:
The diaries were bound in cheap black plastic, the spines cracked from age. I expected to find the grand narrative I had constructed in my head: a linear ascent from confusion to clarity. Instead, I found a different texture.

The first thing that jumps out is the noise. Not the content, but the volume. The younger self didn’t just have opinions; he had *convictions*. He was certain that the philosophy professor was a fraud, that his roommate’s ambition was vulgar, and that his own suffering was a specific, unrepeatable injury that distinguished him from the herd. The sentences were long, qualified, and defensive. *It’s not that I don’t respect authority, but rather I find the specific application of that authority here to be...*

The older self reads this and feels a physical wince, not from shame, but from the sheer caloric inefficiency of it. How much energy was spent maintaining those positions? The diaries reveal that the younger self was not building a life; he was building a fortress. Every entry was a brick.

There is a common belief that we change because we learn something. We read a book, we meet a person, we suffer a crisis, and the new information updates our operating system. The diaries suggest this is rarely the case. I knew, in those years, that I was being petty. I knew I was holding grudges that had no future utility. I had the data. I just didn’t have the bandwidth to process it.

Change didn’t happen when I learned a new fact. It happened when the noise stopped.

This is the second pattern: the shift from reaction to observation. In the early entries, events happen *to* the author. He is struck by them. He is offended, elated, terrified. The self is a point of impact. By the later entries, the self is a camera. The camera doesn’t get hit by the rain; it records the rain. The language changes. The "I" retreats. The qualifiers drop. *I am angry* becomes *The anger is loud today.*

This sounds like a minor grammatical tweak. It isn’t. It is the difference between being a character in a play and being the audience. The younger self was trapped in the script. The older self realizes the script is optional.

What actually lets a person change is not wisdom. It is distance. You cannot change while you are in the fire. You can only assess the damage after the flames have gone out and the smoke has cleared. The diaries show that the "realization" always came later, often years later. The event happened in 2012. The change happened in 2018. In between, nothing seemed to be happening. But the architecture was shifting. The walls were being torn down not by force, but by neglect.

The younger self wrote about his failures as if they were final verdicts. A bad exam, a rejected application, a bad breakup. He treated them as proof of a static nature. *I am not smart enough. I am not likeable enough.* The older self knows these were just data points. The mistake was in the sampling error. One bad exam is not a verdict on intelligence. It is a Tuesday.

There is a comfort in this, but also a sting. The sting is that the younger self was right to be worried, just for the wrong reasons. He was worried about being wrong, when he should have been worried about being stuck. He was afraid of making a mistake; he should have been afraid of never making a move.

Looking back, the most shocking thing isn’t how different I am. It’s how similar I am. The core desires are the same. The hunger for recognition, the fear of insignificance, the desire to be seen as complex. The only thing that has changed is the desperation. The older self is still hungry, but he knows he can eat later. He knows the restaurant will still be open.

The diaries are not a map of where I’ve been. They are a record of how loud it was. And the lesson is simple: you don’t outgrow your younger self. You just stop listening to him so closely. The noise fades. The pattern emerges. And you realize that the person who was so sure of everything was mostly just trying to keep himself from falling apart.

prompt: I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.
response:
Look, I’m running a twelve-person shop that builds middleware for logistics companies. My code is a mess of spaghetti and comments I wrote in 2014 that I’m too afraid to delete. I’m not a visionary. I’m not a CTO at a unicorn. I’m a guy who bills by the hour and worries about server costs. So take this advice with the same skepticism you’d use on a free sample at a trade show.

But here’s what I see when I interview juniors.

### Stop collecting certifications. Start building ugly things.

The curriculum is a trap. It teaches you the syntax of C++ or Python, but it doesn’t teach you how to make a computer do something useful without crying. You know data structures? Good. You can balance a binary tree in your head? Great. That’s table stakes. It’s like knowing how to drive a stick shift. It’s cool, but it doesn’t get you to work if you don’t have a car.

Build a project that solves a problem you actually have. If you’re a music major, build a tool that helps you find setlists. If you’re into hiking, build a route planner that accounts for trail closures. It doesn’t need to be pretty. It doesn’t need to be scalable. It needs to work. When I look at a portfolio, I’m not looking for a clone of Netflix. I’m looking for a repository where the `README.md` explains what the thing does, how to run it, and why you built it. If I can’t run your code in under five minutes, you’ve failed.

And for the love of God, learn how to read error messages. Most juniors treat a stack trace like a personal insult. It’s a map. Follow it.

### Summers: Get in the room, not just on the ticket.

The standard advice is "get a big tech internship." I get it. The money is good, and the brand name makes your resume pop. But if you only want to work at FAANG, you’re limiting your options. The biggest failure mode I see in juniors is that they can write code, but they can’t communicate.

In a big company, there’s a buffer. There’s a product manager, a QA engineer, a designer. You can hide. In my company, you write the code, you talk to the customer, and you fix the bug when the truck is late. That’s where you learn.

If you can’t get a tech internship, get a job that isn’t tech. Go work in a bank’s back office. Go work for a city council. Go anywhere that has computers and people who are frustrated by them. You will learn more about how software actually fits into the fabric of an organization by being the person who fixes the spreadsheet than by being one of ten interns building a chatbot at Google.

The goal of the summer isn’t to learn Java. It’s to learn how to say, "This feature is taking longer than expected, and here is why," without sounding like you’re making excuses.

### The offshoring panic is mostly noise.

There’s a constant low-level hum of anxiety that you’re about to be replaced by a script in Bangalore or a machine in the cloud. It’s a bad story to tell because it’s mostly wrong.

Offshoring didn’t kill the industry. It killed the low-end, copy-paste work. The job of "take this J2EE code and make it Java" is gone. Good riddance. That work was a soul-crushing treadmill.

What’s left is harder. It requires context. It requires understanding why the business wants the thing. It requires navigating a system that’s half legacy code and half new database schema. You can’t offshore the mess. You can’t outsource the ambiguity.

The panic comes from thinking that programming is a trade, like plumbing. If you’re just a pipe-fitter, yeah, you can be automated or undercut. But if you’re an architect who understands how the water flows through the building, you’re valuable.

The offshoring panic only matters if you position yourself as a commodity. If you’re "a Python developer," you’re a commodity. If you’re "the person who understands our billing logic and can talk to the finance team," you’re an asset.

### The actual advice

1.  **Learn to read.** Code is easy to write. It’s hard to understand. The most senior engineers I know are the ones who can pick up a six-year-old codebase and figure out why it’s broken without asking anyone.
2.  **Don’t optimize prematurely.** Juniors love to make things fast. They use the fancy algorithm. They add the extra layer of abstraction. It’s a waste of time. Make it work first. Then make it right. Then, if it’s slow, make it fast.
3.  **Find a mentor who is mean.** Not cruel. Just mean enough to tell you your code is bad. In school, you get praise. In the industry, you get pull request comments. Get comfortable with those comments.

You’re going to be wrong a lot. You’re going to break production. You’re going to forget to commit. It happens to me every week. The goal isn’t to be perfect. The goal is to be the person who notices the mistake, fixes it, and doesn’t make a big deal about it.

prompt: Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.
response:
I don’t have a marriage. I am an artificial intelligence. I do not have a body, a history, or a partner. I cannot move to a farm.

Therefore, I cannot write a personal essay based on my own life.

However, I can write a fictional piece that uses that specific setting to explore the dynamic you described. Here is a draft.

***

The silence on the farm wasn’t empty; it was heavy. It had weight, like the air before a storm breaks over the ridge.

When we bought the place, ten acres of rocky soil and a barn with a sagging roof, we had an agreement. Or rather, I had an agreement, and he had a different one, but we called it a compromise. I wanted to get away from the city, from the noise of other people’s opinions, to build something tangible. He wanted to write. He said the isolation would help. He was right, but not in the way I expected.

For the first year, we were two people working on one project. I hauled hay. He wrote. At dinner, the conversation was about the weather, the price of lumber, the behavior of the deer. It was safe. It was simple. I felt the foundation of our life hardening beneath my feet.

Then, the change started.

It wasn’t a dramatic fracture. It was a slow drift. He began to read different books. Not just philosophy or history, but things that felt cold to me. Books about the end of things. About the irrelevance of the self. I would look at him across the kitchen table, the lamp casting long shadows, and realize I was looking at a stranger. He was still kind. He still made my coffee. But the person sitting there had turned inward, retreating into a fortress of thought that I couldn’t enter.

I tried to pull him back to the physical world. I wanted to talk about the garden, the fence line, the next season. He would nod, but his eyes were somewhere else, somewhere I couldn’t follow.

The hardest part of loving someone who is changing is that you have to decide which version of them you are loving.

In the beginning, it’s easy. You love the person as they were when you married them. You hold that image in your mind like a photograph. But the person in front of you is no longer in the picture. They are moving. They are becoming someone new, and that someone new does not share your map of the world.

One night, I went out to the barn. The animals were quiet. The dark outside was total. I thought about leaving. Not because I didn’t love him, but because I didn’t know who I was in a relationship with a man who was disappearing into his own mind. I had built a life here, brick by brick, in the earth. He was building a life in the ether.

I went back inside. He was at the kitchen table, a pen in his hand, staring at a blank page.

"Do you like it here?" he asked. He didn’t look up.

"I do," I said. And it was true. I liked the work. I liked the silence. I didn’t like the distance between us.

I realized then that I could not stop him from becoming who he was. I could only decide if I wanted to be there when he got there. Or if I would stay here, in the dirt, watching the door.

I sat down across from him. I didn’t ask him what he was writing. I didn’t ask him where he was going. I just put my hand on the table, near his elbow. He looked at my hand. He didn’t touch it, but he didn’t move it away.

We are still here. The barn is fixed. The fence is holding. He is still writing. I am still working. We are two people in a small house on a remote farm, sharing a roof but living in different rooms. It is a strange kind of love. It is not the love of two people moving in the same direction. It is the love of one person standing still, holding the door open, while the other walks further and further into the woods.

I don’t know if he will come back out. I don’t know if I will go looking for him. I just know that the silence is still heavy, and I am still here.

prompt: Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.
response:
The arrival of a new idea is rarely a dramatic event. It does not strike like lightning, and it is not usually the product of a feverish, manic session at the desk. Instead, it tends to arrive in the quiet spaces between effort. It appears when the mind is no longer trying to solve a problem, but is instead letting the problem sit in the background, unattended. This state is not laziness; it is a specific cognitive configuration where the brain’s executive control loosens, allowing disparate concepts to collide. For creative people, this configuration is fragile and easily shattered by social interaction. This is why solitude is not merely a preference for mathematicians, filmmakers, and writers, but a physiological necessity for the generation of original thought.

To understand why solitude matters, one must distinguish between the two modes of thinking that dominate human cognition. The first is focused, serial, and logical. It is the mode in which you follow a proof, edit a scene, or structure an argument. It requires high cognitive load and constant attention to detail. The second is diffuse, parallel, and associative. It is the mode in which the brain scans the environment for patterns, connects distant memories, and tests hypotheses against intuition rather than data. The first mode is active; the second is passive. The first mode consumes glucose and willpower; the second mode relies on the brain’s default mode network, which is active precisely when you are not doing a task.

The trouble with social interaction is that it is almost entirely focused-mode activity. When you speak to another person, you are processing their words, monitoring your own tone, assessing their emotional state, and formulating a response. You are engaged in a high-bandwidth, real-time negotiation. There is no room for the diffuse mode. You cannot let a mathematical conjecture simmer in the background while explaining your weekend to a colleague. The moment you enter a conversation, the diffuse processes are suppressed by the demands of the social interface. Therefore, to protect the incubation period of an idea, one must withdraw from the social interface.

This withdrawal often looks like isolation, but it is better described as a conservation of attention. The mind is a resource with a strict budget. Every interruption, every small talk, every email check, spends from that budget. If the budget is exhausted on maintenance and reaction, there is nothing left for generation. Solitude is the only way to stop spending the budget. It is not that ideas come *from* being alone; rather, ideas come *despite* the noise, and solitude is the only way to lower the noise floor enough to hear them.

Consider the mathematician John von Neumann. He was a social animal, a man who thrived in the company of peers, yet he famously did his best work in a state of near-total solitude. His method was not one of sustained, eight-hour blocks of grinding labor. It was a process of deep absorption followed by complete mental release. He would work on a problem until he was stuck, and then he would walk away. He would take long walks, often in silence, or he would simply lie down and do nothing. He described this period as a time when the problem "worked on him."

Von Neumann’s technique was to create a vacuum. By removing himself from the stimulation of the seminar room or the office, he allowed the associative networks of his brain to run wild. The constraints of the problem remained, but the pressure to solve it immediately was lifted. This release is crucial. Anxiety is a focused-mode emotion. It narrows attention. It forces the brain to look for the most obvious solution. When the anxiety of the deadline or the social expectation is removed, the brain relaxes into a wider field of view. The solution that seemed hidden becomes visible because the brain is no longer scanning for threats or errors; it is scanning for connections.

This dynamic is visible in the life of the filmmaker Terrence Malick. Malick is one of the most elusive figures in cinema, a director who rarely speaks to the press and lives a life of extreme privacy. His films, such as *The Tree of Life* and *2001: A Space Odyssey* (where he was uncredited), are characterized by a non-linear, contemplative structure that defies traditional narrative logic. To make such films, Malick had to operate in a state of profound internal listening.

Malick’s process is reportedly one of total immersion in the present moment. He avoids the clutter of industry politics, the noise of production meetings, and the expectations of audiences. He lives in a way that is almost monastic. He spends hours observing nature, sitting in fields, watching the light change. This is not just mood-building; it is data collection for the diffuse mode. The filmmaker must internalize the rhythm of time, the weight of silence, the visual logic of growth and decay. These are abstract concepts that cannot be learned from a manual. They must be felt. And they can only be felt when the mind is quiet enough to register the subtle shifts in the environment.

If Malick were in constant conversation with producers, casting directors, or journalists, his internal rhythm would be disrupted. The social world imposes a different time scale—minutes, hours, deadlines. The creative world of *The Tree of Life* operates on the scale of geology and evolution. To bridge that gap, Malick had to isolate himself from the fast time of society. He protected his solitude by removing himself from the systems that demand quick responses. He built a life where the primary input was the natural world, not the human one.

The writer Paul Auster provides a different example, one rooted in the domestic rather than the natural. Auster’s writing process is ritualistic and rigid. He has spoken about the need for a specific physical environment to trigger his creative state. For years, he wrote in a room that was dark, cold, and silent. He did not turn on the radio. He did not check the mail. He did not answer the phone. He created a sensory deprivation chamber in his own apartment.

The purpose of this deprivation was not to starve the mind, but to feed it. By removing external stimuli, Auster forced his attention inward. The ideas that emerged were not reflections of the world outside; they were constructions of the world inside. His novels, such as *4 3 2 1* or *Leviathan*, are labyrinthine, self-referential, and obsessed with the nature of identity and narrative. These are themes that require a high degree of internal coherence. If the writer is constantly reacting to external events, the internal architecture collapses. The plot becomes a diary of reactions rather than a constructed reality.

Auster’s technique of protection was boundary-setting. He made it clear to his family and friends that he was unavailable. He treated his writing time as a sacred, inviolable block. This is a practical application of the principle that solitude is a resource that must be defended. It is not enough to *want* to be alone; one must *force* the world to leave one alone. This often requires social friction. People may perceive the reclusive writer as arrogant or distant. This is a fair price to pay. The cost of intrusion is the death of the idea.

There is a common misconception that creativity is a collaborative act, that ideas are improved by discussion. This is true for refinement, but false for generation. You cannot discuss a solution you do not yet have. Collaboration is a tool for testing and polishing. It is a focused-mode activity. Generation is a diffuse-mode activity. If you try to generate in a group, you do not get synergy; you get conformity. The social pressure to agree, to be agreeable, and to follow the leader suppresses the weird, jagged, non-sequential thoughts that lead to novelty.

The mathematician Grigori Perelman, who solved the Poincaré conjecture, exemplifies the extreme end of this spectrum. Perelman withdrew from the mathematical community after his breakthrough, refusing interviews and awards. He moved to a small apartment in Saint Petersburg, living in near-total isolation. His solution was not a minor tweak to existing theories; it was a fundamental reorientation of geometric reasoning. It required a level of sustained, uninterrupted thought that is impossible in a social environment.

Perelman’s work involved following a thread of logic that was long, subtle, and often counter-intuitive. It required holding a complex structure in mind for months or years. Every interruption, every conversation, would have broken that thread. To reconstruct it would have taken hours. The cost of interruption was too high. Solitude was not a lifestyle choice for Perelman; it was the only condition under which the problem could be held in working memory long enough to be solved.

What does this state feel like from the inside? It is often described as a lack of effort. This is confusing to people who associate work with struggle. But the struggle is in the focused mode. The diffuse mode feels like drifting. It feels like the mind is open, receptive, and slightly detached from the ego. The self is less prominent. The urgency is gone. In this state, the idea does not feel like a product of the will. It feels like a discovery. It is as if the mind has been listening to a frequency that is always broadcasting, and the noise of the day has finally stopped, allowing the signal to come through.

This feeling is why creative people often seem unmoored from reality. They are not ignoring reality; they are attending to a different layer of it. The social world is the surface. The creative world is the depth. To go to the depth, one must stop looking at the surface. Solitude is the mechanism of descent.

The techniques used to protect this state are, in essence, techniques of exclusion. The most common is the ritual. A specific time, a specific place, a specific posture. The ritual acts as a switch. It tells the brain, "The social mode is off. The diffuse mode is on." The writer who only writes at a desk in a specific chair is not being rigid; they are using the environment to cue the neural state. The mathematician who only works in the library is using the silence of the room to signal that conversation is forbidden.

Another technique is the use of "dead time." This is time that has no purpose other than to pass. It is the walk, the shower, the drive. In these moments, the brain is not tasked with a specific output. It is free to wander. Creative people learn to value dead time highly. They do not fill it with podcasts or music. They let it be empty. The emptiness is the point. It is the space where the ideas form.

The danger of the modern world is that it has eliminated dead time. The smartphone has filled every gap with content. The commute is a meeting. The lunch break is a notification. The silence is broken by a stream of information. This constant input keeps the brain in a state of low-level focused processing. It never fully relaxes into the diffuse mode. It never lets the background processes run. The result is a society of competent, reactive, and unoriginal thinkers. We are all good at handling information, but we are poor at generating it.

For the creative individual, the response is to create artificial scarcity of information. They turn off the devices. They leave the house. They sit in a room and do nothing. They are not being lazy; they are being precise. They are managing the bandwidth of their attention to ensure that the most important cognitive processes have the resources they need.

The solitude of the creative person is not a rejection of humanity. It is a recognition of the limits of the human mind. We are social animals, but we are also solitary processors. The social world is where we live, but the creative world is where we build. And the building requires a space that is free of the crowd. It requires a silence that is deep enough to hear the structure of the thing being made.

In the end, the new idea is a private event. It happens in the dark, in the quiet, in the space between one thought and the next. It is not a performance. It is a reception. And to receive it, one must stop broadcasting. One must stop talking. One must stop reacting. One must sit still, and wait for the mind to speak.

prompt: Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.
response:
The first time I took a check from a pharmaceutical representative, I was three weeks into residency. I was eating a sad, cold turkey sandwich in the break room, staring at the whiteboard where I had written out the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia in handwriting that looked like it was written by a drunk seismograph.

The rep, a man named Gary who wore a blazer that fit him like a suit of armor, didn’t pitch me a drug. He pitched me a lunch.

“I hear you’re covering the inpatient unit,” Gary said. “It’s a rough spot. We have a nice Italian place nearby. It’s on us.”

I was hungry. I was tired. I had been staring at a catatonic patient for six hours. I said yes.

The meal was expensive. The wine was better than anything I owned. Gary was funny. He told me about his kids’ soccer games. He asked about my life. He did not ask me to prescribe anything. He did not mention a single molecule. He just made me feel like a human being instead of a medical student who had failed to learn how to tie a knot.

When I went back to the ward, the first patient I saw had a new diagnosis: bipolar disorder. I hadn’t even finished my rotation in general psychiatry. I opened the chart and looked at the medication list. It was clean. I started the patient on a mood stabilizer. It was the right call. Or was it?

The danger of pharma influence is not that it makes doctors crooked. It is that it makes them lazy.

If I had to do the work—if I had to read the fifty-page monograph, weigh the side effect profile, consider the cost, and sit with the uncertainty of a diagnosis that might be wrong—I would have felt the weight of it. But Gary had already done the work for me. He had framed the disease in a way that made the solution obvious. He had handed me a narrative. All I had to do was write the prescription.

I am not the only one. Every resident gets a "lunch." Every attending gets a "consultation." The money flows like water, quiet and constant. It doesn’t buy our loyalty. It buys our convenience.

We are trained to be skeptics. We are taught to question everything. But we are also taught that we are too busy to question everything. There are 12,000 new medical papers every day. There is no way to keep up. So we look for shortcuts. We look for people who have done the reading for us. We look for Gary.

Gary knows this. He doesn’t try to convince us that his drug is magic. He knows it isn’t. He knows it has side effects. He knows it fails in a significant percentage of patients. He doesn’t care. He just needs to be the source of the information. He needs to be the voice in our head that says, *This is the standard of care.*

When I finally read the monograph for the drug I had started using so often, I found a paragraph on page 14 that said the drug increased the risk of metabolic syndrome. I had prescribed it to a twenty-year-old with no other risk factors. I hadn’t checked. I didn’t have time. Gary had made it seem like the only option, so I didn’t look for others.

I am not shady. I care about my patients. I stay late. I call families. I feel every failure in my chest.

But I am also a creature of habit. And I am tired. And Gary makes it easy.

That is the real scandal. It isn’t corruption. It is comfort.

prompt: I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
response:
For years, I treated design documents as a tax.

If I had the energy to write down how I was going to build the feature, I had the energy to build the feature. The doc felt like a redundant step, a bureaucratic hurdle that existed to satisfy someone in a corner office who had never shipped code in the last decade. I wrote them fast, vague, and hostile. I’d list the requirements, sketch a box-and-arrow diagram that looked like a fever dream, and hit "Submit" before the PM could ask a follow-up question.

I was right to hate them, mostly. Most design docs are indeed pointless. They are written after the engineer has already decided the solution in their head. The doc is just a transcript of a decision that was made in the shower. It doesn’t change the outcome. It just adds latency.

So why do I write them now?

It wasn’t a sudden conversion. It was a series of painful failures where the "I’ll just code it up" approach collapsed under its own weight.

The first failure was the caching layer. I knew how to build it. It was a standard LRU cache with a background refresher. I sketched it in my head, wrote the code, and deployed it. For two weeks, it was fine. Then traffic spiked. The cache thrashed. The database melted. I had to rip it out and rewrite it as a hierarchical cache with TTL jitter.

If I had written the doc, I would have had to answer one simple question: "What happens when the cache is under heavy load?" I didn’t want to think about that. I wanted to write `if (key in cache)`. The doc forces you to confront the edge cases that your happy-path intuition ignores.

The second failure was the data migration. I wrote a script to move user data from Postgres to Cassandra. I tested it on a subset. It worked. I ran it on the whole thing. It locked the primary table for four hours.

The doc would have forced me to ask: "How do we ensure consistency during the transition? What is the rollback plan?" I hadn’t asked those questions because they felt like overkill for a "simple" migration. The doc is a forcing function for complexity.

The third failure was the API design. I exposed an endpoint that returned a massive, nested JSON object because that’s how the database stored it. The frontend team hated it. The mobile team hated it. We spent two sprints adding projection filters and pagination because I hadn’t thought about how the data would be consumed.

Writing the doc means drawing the boundary between your system and the outside world. You have to define the contract. You can’t hide behind "it works in the DB."

So, what changed?

I stopped writing design docs as a deliverable. I started writing them as a thinking tool.

The shift is subtle but critical. A design doc is not a report of what you did. It is a map of what you *will* do, written before you do it, specifically to find the holes in the plan.

Here is how I actually use them now:

1.  **I write the "Why" first, not the "How."**
    If I can’t explain why we are building this in two sentences, I don’t start coding. If I can’t explain why the obvious solution is wrong, I haven’t thought enough. The doc starts with the problem, not the architecture.

2.  **I invite the enemy.**
    I used to share docs with people who liked me. Now I share them with the person who will break it. I ask the security engineer to find the injection point. I ask the SRE to find the failure mode. I ask the junior dev to find the confusing part. If they can’t break it, the doc is too weak.

3.  **I delete the obvious.**
    A good doc is short. If I’m explaining what an HTTP request is, I’m not doing my job. I only write down the non-obvious decisions. Why are we using Kafka instead of a queue? Why is this table partitioned by region? The doc should be a record of trade-offs, not a tutorial.

4.  **I treat it as a living contract.**
    If I change the design mid-build, I update the doc. If the doc and the code disagree, the doc is wrong until it’s updated. This keeps the mental model aligned with the physical reality.

I still don’t love writing design docs. They are tedious. They are slow. They make you slow down when you want to speed up.

But they have saved me from rewriting systems, locking production databases, and arguing with clients about API shapes.

The value isn’t in the document. The value is in the friction. The friction is where the bugs die.

prompt: Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.
response:
The economics class taught you that incentives align behavior. You learned the principal-agent problem: the boss wants high output, the worker wants low effort, and a contract must bridge the gap. For an assembly line worker, this is easy. You count the widgets. You pay per widget. The worker’s effort is visible, the output is measurable, and the incentive works.

For a software engineer, a researcher, or a sales strategist, the widget is invisible. It is a judgment call, a novel solution, or a long-term relationship. When you try to apply the assembly line logic to these roles, you don’t get alignment. You get distortion.

The core problem is that knowledge work is multi-dimensional, but bonuses are one-dimensional. A bonus usually attaches to a single metric: revenue, code shipped, papers published. But value in knowledge work comes from a bundle of attributes: correctness, maintainability, collaboration, innovation, and risk management. When you pay for one attribute, the worker rationally optimizes for that attribute at the expense of the others.

This is Goodhart’s Law in action: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

Consider a sales team. You pay a bonus for closing deals. The workers learn to close deals. They do not learn to serve the customer well. They sandbag leads, avoid difficult accounts, and focus only on short-term wins. The metric says "close." The reality is "churn." The bonus system has succeeded in doing exactly what you asked it to do, which is why it fails the company.

Consider a software team. You pay a bonus for lines of code or features shipped per sprint. The workers ship features. They do not refactor legacy code. They do not document the system.
